title: Spec-Driven Development with OpenSpec and GitHub Copilot
text:
Preface
AI-assisted development with tools like GitHub Copilot can be easy to start and difficult to control. A prompt can produce a plausible implementation in minutes, but plausibility is not the same as correctness. The hard questions remain: What are we building? Which parts of the existing system matter? How will we know that the result matches the intent?
This book is for software engineers, technical leads, and architects who want better answers to those questions without turning every change into a heavyweight ceremony. It introduces Spec-Driven Development (SDD) with OpenSpec as a practical way to make intent explicit, keep requirements close to implementation, and give GitHub Copilot the project context it needs. The examples move from greenfield work to brownfield systems, then through the less glamorous parts of real delivery: drift, verification, archiving, governance, and troubleshooting.
The approach has costs. Writing a useful spec takes time, and a vague or oversized spec can slow a team down instead of helping it. OpenSpec does not remove judgment from engineering, and Copilot can still misunderstand both the code and the specification. The goal is not to add paperwork for its own sake. It is to create a small, inspectable record of intent that helps people and tools make fewer expensive assumptions.
This book presents Spec-Driven Development (SDD) as a practical response to that continuity problem. It uses OpenSpec to keep requirements, proposed changes, design decisions, and implementation tasks in the repository where developers and agents can review them together.
The running example is a commercial truck search application. Its requirements change over three 90-minute mornings: the team first searches by a 15-character unit number, then adds VIN search, then shortens the unit-number limit and revises an active filter proposal. The changes are small enough to follow, but they expose the coordination problems that appear in larger systems.
This is not an argument for writing a specification before every code edit. Small, local, reversible changes may not justify the overhead. The workflow earns its cost when behavior crosses layers, requirements are likely to change, or several people and agent sessions need the same account of what the system should do.
Each part mirrors one morning of the training class. You can read the book independently or use its exercises as the class lab guide.

title: 1  From Chat Sessions to Durable Intent
text:
1.1 A request that looks complete
Suppose a Jira story asks a developer to add exact search by a 15-character truck unit number across a Spring Boot backend and an Angular frontend. The developer gives the story to Copilot and asks it to implement the change.
Copilot can generate plausible code, but the request leaves basic behavior unsettled. It does not say whether matching is case-sensitive, which characters are valid, what the API returns when no unit matches, or how the interface reports invalid input. The agent may need to stop and ask questions or make choices that look reasonable. If those choices remain in the chat, the pull request may contain working code without a reviewable account of the behavior the team accepted.
A later developer inherits the code and tests, but not necessarily the reasoning behind them. A new Copilot session faces the same limit: it can inspect what the first session built, but it cannot reliably distinguish an intentional business rule from an assumption that survived implementation.

title: 1  From Chat Sessions to Durable Intent
text:
1.2 The same request with OpenSpec
In a spec-driven workflow, the team records unsettled behavior before asking Copilot to implement it. An OpenSpec proposal states the goal and scope, while requirements and scenarios describe observable behavior. Technical choices that affect the implementation may belong in a design, and a task list connects that intent to the work.
These artifacts can give reviewers a stable target before the code exists. Later Copilot sessions can draw on accepted decisions in the repository instead of the full history of a conversation. The team can then check code and tests against the specification rather than whichever interpretation an agent chose.
This approach does not make the decisions correct or remove the need for engineering judgment. It changes where the decisions live, when the team can review them, and how readily another person can recover them after the original chat session ends.

1.4 The running example
The book builds a unit-search capability for a fictional application in the Penske maintenance portfolio. The example is small enough to keep the focus on the workflow, but broad enough to cover greenfield and brownfield development, changes to accepted specifications, and revisions to work already in progress.

The backend uses Java 21 and Spring Boot 4.x.
The frontend uses Angular 21 and TypeScript.
The backend and frontend live in separate Bitbucket repositories, each with its own OpenSpec history.
The first request asks for search by a 15-character truck unit number but leaves several behaviors unsettled.

The missing decisions make the coordination problem concrete: matching rules, invalid input, no-match behavior, response shape, and the boundary between the two repositories. Later chapters add VIN search, change accepted unit-number behavior, revise an active change, and coordinate parallel work. Each step tests whether the specification can connect the team’s previous intent to its next decision.

1.6 The coordination problem
An agent’s ability to generate an implementation does not mean the team has agreed about the behavior. Tests provide evidence about the implementation, but only against the expectations they encode. A generated test may repeat the same unsupported assumption as the generated production code.
Separate artifacts can make those concerns easier to review. The specification records what the team has agreed to build. The implementation attempts to satisfy that agreement, while tests and other verification provide evidence about whether it does. With those roles distinct, a reviewer may be better able to identify whether a disagreement belongs in the requirement, the code, or the evidence.

1.7 Jira, chat, and repository artifacts
Each artifact has a different job. Jira tracks the request, ownership, priority, and delivery status. OpenSpec records proposed behavior, changes to accepted requirements, design decisions, and implementation tasks. Code implements those decisions, while tests and review produce evidence about the result.
A chat transcript can help during exploration, but it may mix questions, discarded alternatives, and accepted decisions. When the transcript becomes the specification, a later reader must reconstruct which statements still apply. Issue identifiers and links can connect the artifacts without requiring Jira API automation in this book.

section: 1.8 When a specification earns its cost
text:
1.8 When a specification earns its cost
Before choosing the workflow, consider change risk, ambiguity, coordination cost, and reversibility. A full specification may make sense when behavior crosses the backend and frontend, requirements may change, or multiple developers and agent sessions need the same account of intent. A smaller record or direct edit may be enough when the change is local, obvious, and easy to reverse.
A specification also has a cost. The team needs to review it, update it when decisions change, and keep it consistent with the implemented behavior. Without that maintenance, OpenSpec can become ceremony or stale documentation. The aim is to record enough intent for the risk and coordination demands of the change, rather than to maximize the number of artifacts.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
text:
2.1 Learning objective
Open an OpenSpec repository during an active change and you may find two accounts of the product. One records the behavior the team accepts now. The other proposes a different state and records the reasoning and work needed to reach it.
Both accounts need to remain visible. If a draft requirement immediately replaced an accepted one, another developer or agent could mistake a proposal for shipped behavior. If the proposal lived only in chat, reviewers could lose its scope or struggle to tell which decisions survived discussion. OpenSpec keeps accepted specifications and active changes in separate directories, then brings them together when the team archives completed work, as shown in the OpenSpec quickstart1.
This separation is the center of the operating model. The rest of the workflow helps a team answer four questions:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to read an OpenSpec repository as a map of accepted behavior and proposed changes. You should also be able to place rationale, requirements, design decisions, and tasks in the artifacts where reviewers can evaluate them.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
section: 2.2 Read the tree as two kinds of truth
text:
2.2 Read the tree as two kinds of truth
Start with the two directories that carry most of the workflow:
openspec/
|-- specs/
|   `-- <capability>/
|       `-- spec.md
`-- changes/
    |-- <active-change>/
    |   |-- proposal.md
    |   |-- specs/
    |   |   `-- <capability>/
    |   |       `-- spec.md
    |   |-- design.md
    |   `-- tasks.md
    `-- archive/
        `-- <completed-change>/
Ask a different question of each location:

In openspec/specs/, ask, “What behavior has the team accepted as the current baseline?”
In openspec/changes/<active-change>/, ask, “What difference is under consideration or implementation?”
In openspec/changes/archive/, ask, “Which completed change explains how the baseline reached its current form?”

Suppose the accepted specifications say nothing about searching by truck unit number. A new folder named add-unit-number-search can describe that proposed capability without making it part of the baseline. During review and implementation, the main specs and the change may intentionally disagree because the change contains a delta, not a second complete copy of the product specification.
That temporary disagreement gives reviewers a useful comparison: would applying this delta produce the intended behavior? After the implementation passes review and verification, the archive operation can merge the delta into openspec/specs/ and move the change folder under openspec/changes/archive/.






NoteA repository is not proof



Treat the tree as a record of claims and decisions, not as proof that the software behaves as written. Tests, review, and runtime checks still need to supply evidence. OpenSpec gives that evidence a stated target.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
section: 2.3 Follow one change through its artifacts
text:
2.3 Follow one change through its artifacts
The default spec-driven schema uses four planning artifacts. Their dependency order follows the decisions a team needs to make: proposal first; specs and design after the proposal; tasks after both; implementation after the task list. The default spec-driven schema reference2 documents these roles and the conditions under which specs or design may be skipped.
                         +-- delta specs --+
proposal.md -------------+                  +-- tasks.md -- apply
                         +-- design.md -----+
The dependency order exposes omissions. If the task list requires an API decision that does not appear in the design, pause before coding. If a design choice changes user-visible behavior but no requirement records it, return to the delta spec. If a delta introduces a capability that the proposal never names, revisit the proposal’s scope.

2.3.1 Proposal: why this change, and how far does it reach?
Use proposal.md to frame the decision. For unit-number search, it might identify the need for exact search, name the affected capability, describe the impact on the backend and frontend, and exclude partial matching from the first change.
A controller class, SQL predicate, or Angular component probably does not belong here. Those details pull the proposal toward implementation before reviewers have agreed on the problem and scope.
A useful proposal should let a reviewer challenge the change at low cost:

Does this solve the right problem?
Is the proposed capability too broad or too narrow?
Which existing capabilities would change?
What would remain outside the change?



2.3.2 Delta spec: what observable behavior would change?
Place behavioral differences under the change’s specs/ directory, with one spec.md for each capability named by the proposal. OpenSpec delta sections distinguish ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED, and RENAMED requirements. Requirements and scenarios describe what a user or another system could observe, not the code structure that might produce it.
For the running example, a delta could say that a valid 15-character unit number returns exact matches. Its scenarios could cover a match, no match, and invalid input. The delta need not name a Spring repository method or an Angular form control unless that name is part of an external contract.
When a statement feels misplaced, use a replacement test: could the team replace Spring Data with another persistence mechanism while preserving the statement? If so, the statement may describe behavior and belong in the spec. If the replacement would make the statement irrelevant while behavior stayed the same, move it to the design or task list.


2.3.3 Design: how might the implementation satisfy the behavior?
Use design.md when the technical approach deserves review before coding. Cross-repository contracts, a new dependency, data-model changes, security constraints, migrations, or a consequential trade-off may justify it. A small change with an obvious implementation may not.
For unit-number search, the design might choose an endpoint shape, assign validation responsibilities between Angular and Spring Boot, or record how both repositories will keep response semantics consistent. It may also preserve rejected alternatives and their costs so that a later agent does not reopen a settled choice without new evidence.
The design may explain how to satisfy the proposed behavior, but it should not quietly create more behavior. If the design makes unit numbers case-insensitive, users or clients can observe that choice, so the delta spec needs the rule too.


2.3.4 Tasks: what work remains, and in what order?
Turn the reviewed behavior and approach into checkable work in tasks.md. The apply phase tracks Markdown checkboxes, so each task should name an outcome that an agent can complete and a reviewer can inspect.
For example:
## 1. Backend search contract

- [ ] 1.1 Add request validation for the accepted unit-number rules.
- [ ] 1.2 Implement exact-match search and response mapping.
- [ ] 1.3 Add tests for match, no-match, and invalid-input scenarios.
A checked box records claimed progress, not verification evidence. A test result, review, or runtime observation must support the claim.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
section: 2.4 Move through the loop with review points
text:
2.4 Move through the loop with review points
The OpenSpec quickstart presents a five-step loop: explore, propose, review, apply, and archive. Optional skills may add explicit update, sync, and verify operations, but the same review points remain useful. The OpenSpec skills reference3 distinguishes the core skills from optional profile-installed skills and states what each skill may create or change.

2.4.1 Explore without pretending the plan is settled
Use exploration to inspect the codebase, find existing behavior, compare options, and surface unanswered questions. In the unit-search change, exploration might reveal that the backend already normalizes identifiers while the frontend validates only length. That finding could change the proposal, but exploration need not create artifacts or code.
Stay in exploration while an unanswered question could change scope or behavior. Move to proposal once the team can state the problem and the affected capabilities without asking the agent to fill gaps silently.


2.4.2 Propose, then review the artifacts
Proposal turns the idea into reviewable files. Read them before implementation in an order that follows their dependencies:

Read proposal.md for purpose, scope, and affected capabilities.
Read the delta specs for observable behavior and edge cases.
Read design.md, when present, for technical decisions and trade-offs.
Read tasks.md for coverage, dependency order, and stopping points.

When review finds a defect, change the artifact that owns the decision and then inspect its dependents. A revised requirement may require a design change; a revised design may require different tasks. Editing only the task list could leave Copilot with contradictory instructions.


2.4.3 Apply from the plan, but allow the plan to be wrong
During apply, the agent reads the change artifacts, implements pending tasks, and marks completed checkboxes. This supports work across chat sessions because progress and intent remain in the repository instead of one context window.
Do not force implementation through a contradiction. If the codebase disproves a design assumption or exposes missing behavior, stop and revise the affected artifact. An active change can evolve; its first draft does not have to survive contact with the code.


2.4.4 Verify against the change, not only the task list
Before archive, compare the delta’s required behavior with the implementation and the evidence from tests or inspection. A complete task list with an unimplemented scenario should block archive. So should passing tests that encode behavior the team never accepted.
Verification may use OpenSpec’s optional verification skill, project test commands, manual checks, or a combination suited to the risk. Whatever the mechanism, check that each requirement has evidence and that the implementation did not introduce behavior outside the reviewed scope.


2.4.5 Sync or archive when the baseline should change
Use sync when accepted specifications should absorb a delta while the change remains active. Use archive when the change is complete and its folder can move into completed history. Archive can synchronize outstanding deltas before moving the folder. Warnings about incomplete artifacts or tasks should prompt review rather than automatic dismissal.
After archive, a new session should find the current unit-search behavior in the main specification. The archived change should retain the reason, alternatives, and implementation path behind that behavior.
Git still governs collaboration. OpenSpec artifacts are ordinary repository files, subject to branches, pull requests, code review, and commit history. Each team must decide whether archive occurs before or after merge based on its release and review practice.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
section: 2.5 Distinguish the interface from the operation
text:
2.5 Distinguish the interface from the operation
The same workflow may appear through several interfaces. A terminal command such as openspec validate runs the OpenSpec CLI. A prompt such as /openspec-propose invokes an agent skill in the chat host. Some hosts expose shorter aliases, and optional profiles may install more skills.
Before copying a command, ask:

Does this text belong in the terminal or in Copilot Chat?
Has the repository been initialized with the expected schema and profile?
Does this host use the documented skill name or a host-specific alias?
Will the operation write planning artifacts, application code, accepted specs, or archive history?

The last question sets a practical guardrail. Explore and verify normally inspect and report. Propose writes planning artifacts. Apply writes code and updates task progress. Sync changes accepted specs. Archive changes accepted specs when needed and relocates the completed change. Confirm the expected write boundary before approving an agent action.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
text:
2.6 Hands-on exercise
Classify each statement from the unit-number search change, then name the file that should own it:

Fleet coordinators need to find a truck from the identifier printed on a work order.
A valid unit number contains exactly 15 characters.
The Angular client will reject invalid length before sending a request.
Add controller tests for valid, invalid, match, and no-match cases.
The backend and frontend changes passed their focused test suites.

Some statements need revision before they fit. Statement 1 suggests rationale for proposal.md. Statement 2 describes observable behavior for a delta spec. Statement 3 records an implementation decision for design.md. Statement 4 belongs in tasks.md. Statement 5 supplies verification evidence, which should be recorded with the team’s change or pull-request evidence rather than rewritten as a requirement.
Now move statement 2 into design.md and consider the consequence. A reviewer could no longer approve the behavior without reading the implementation plan, and a later design change could erase a validation rule that users still depend on. Artifact boundaries are review boundaries, not filing conventions.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
text:
2.7 Verification checkpoint
Given an unfamiliar OpenSpec tree, try to answer these questions without reading its application code:

Which behavior represents the accepted baseline?
Which changes remain active, and which capabilities does each touch?
Where would you challenge scope, behavior, technical approach, and work coverage?
Which artifact dependencies remain incomplete?
What evidence would you request before archive?
After archive, where would you look for current behavior and where for its history?

If the tree supports those answers, the operating model is doing useful work. If it does not, inspect whether information is missing, duplicated, or stored in an artifact that asks reviewers to make the wrong decision.

title: 2  The OpenSpec Operating Model
text:
2.8 What you learned
Read openspec/specs/ as the accepted behavioral baseline and openspec/changes/ as proposed differences from it. Within a change, the proposal frames purpose and scope, delta specs define observable behavior, the design records consequential implementation choices, and tasks expose the work still to do.
Treat explore, review, apply, verification, sync, and archive as points where the team can inspect or correct the change. The next chapter examines the artifact that most directly constrains an agent’s guesses: testable requirements and scenarios.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.1 Learning objective
Imagine giving Copilot this Jira story:
What could the agent reasonably infer? It might accept only letters and digits, trim spaces, ignore case, return one truck, return several trucks, or treat no match as an error. Each choice could lead to coherent code and green tests. None of those tests could tell the team whether the agent chose the intended behavior.
Use OpenSpec to expose those choices before they disappear into implementation. Record reviewed behavior in a requirement, make that behavior observable through scenarios, and use a delta to show how the proposal would change the accepted specification. Then ask the agent to work from that bounded target rather than from the Jira sentence alone.
Write and maintain OpenSpec requirements whose scenarios could guide implementation, review, and verification without prescribing REST endpoints, database queries, or Angular components.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
section: 3.2 Start with the decisions hidden in the story
text:
3.2 Start with the decisions hidden in the story
Before asking an agent to draft a specification, mark every phrase that permits more than one reasonable interpretation. For the running example, try questions such as these:

Does 15-character count leading or trailing spaces?
Which characters may appear?
Does exact include case?
Could more than one truck share the same unit number?
How should the system distinguish missing input, invalid input, and no match?
Which result fields may the user or client observe?

Do not turn unanswered questions into confident requirements. Record an owner or a deliberate deferral instead. An agent can draft alternatives, inspect existing behavior, and find related tests, but the team still has to choose product behavior.
A small decision table can keep that boundary visible:



Question
Status
Decision or next action




Required length?
Settled
Exactly 15 characters


Match rule?
Settled
Exact match


Allowed character set?
Open

No-match response?
Open

Do not implement from this table yet. The open rows could still change validation, response handling, and tests, so preserve them as questions until someone with authority resolves them.






WarningA testable sentence can still encode a guess



“The system SHALL return 404 when no truck matches” can be tested, but testability does not make the choice correct. Ask where the behavior came from before asking whether a test could prove it.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
section: 3.3 Write the requirement as a behavioral contract
text:
3.3 Write the requirement as a behavioral contract
Once the decisions have owners and answers, write the proposed difference in the active change’s capability spec. For a change named add-unit-number-search, the file might live here:
openspec/changes/add-unit-number-search/
`-- specs/
    `-- vehicle-search/
        `-- spec.md
OpenSpec delta specs group requirements under ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED, or RENAMED sections. Each requirement needs at least one #### Scenario: block for validation to accept its structure, as described by the OpenSpec CLI reference1.
Suppose an agent converts only the two settled rows into a delta. Its first draft might pass a structural check while still exposing gaps for review:
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Search by unit number

The system SHALL allow a user to search for trucks by an exact 15-character
unit number.

#### Scenario: Matching unit number

- **GIVEN** a truck exists with unit number `TRUCK-000001234`
- **WHEN** the user searches for `TRUCK-000001234`
- **THEN** the system returns that truck
Read the requirement as a contract rather than a design sketch. Test its boundary by replacing a Spring Boot controller with another delivery mechanism or changing the persistence layer. Keep the wording in the spec when those substitutions would leave the promised behavior unchanged.
Next, test the wording against the decision table. The word exact still leaves case handling unclear, and 15-character still leaves whitespace handling unclear. The missing no-match scenario correctly reflects an open decision, but it also blocks implementation of that path. Treat the draft as structurally recognizable and behaviorally incomplete.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.4 Give each scenario one job
Treat a scenario as a small experiment against the requirement. Establish only the state needed for the behavior, perform one action, and name an observable result. Avoid turning the scenario into a transcript of controller calls, SQL execution, or component state changes.
Use each clause to answer a different question:








Clause
Ask
Avoid




GIVEN
What state or input matters before the action?
Setup unrelated to the behavior


WHEN
What does the user or system do?
A chain of implementation steps


THEN
What could a test or reviewer observe?
Private methods or internal data structures



Compare these two scenarios:
#### Scenario: Search executes the repository query

- **GIVEN** the controller receives a unit-number parameter
- **WHEN** the service calls `findByUnitNumber`
- **THEN** the repository executes an equality predicate
#### Scenario: Matching unit number

- **GIVEN** a truck exists with unit number `TRUCK-000001234`
- **WHEN** the user searches for `TRUCK-000001234`
- **THEN** the system returns that truck
Prefer the second version when a repository rename or a move away from Spring Data should leave the behavior unchanged. It describes the result rather than the route taken to produce it. Put the endpoint shape, repository strategy, and Angular component boundaries in design.md when they need review.

3.4.1 Cover decisions, not every imaginable input
Build a scenario matrix from settled rules rather than from a generic checklist. For unit-number search, the matrix might begin like this:

Example
Observable result

Combine rows that produce the same behavior for the same reason. Give a boundary its own scenario when it changes the contract or exposes a known risk. Leave framework checks and repeated implementation details to lower-level tests rather than promoting them to product requirements.
Avoid equating scenario count with confidence. A dozen examples cannot repair an undefined term, and one carefully chosen boundary may constrain an agent better than several happy-path variations.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
section: 3.5 Let the agent draft without letting it decide
text:
3.5 Let the agent draft without letting it decide
Give Copilot the source decisions, the capability boundary, and a prohibition against filling gaps. A prompt for the first draft might look like this:
Draft the delta spec for add-unit-number-search from the attached decision
table. Use ADDED requirements and Given/When/Then scenarios. Describe only
observable behavior. Do not choose answers for open rows; list them after the
draft as blockers. Do not name endpoints, classes, database queries, or Angular
components.
Then review the output by tracing every normative word back to a source. Where did SHALL, exact, invalid, one, or all come from? If the source material does not support the word, remove it or return the question to its owner.
Try asking the agent to challenge its own draft:
For each requirement and scenario, identify:
1. a term with more than one plausible interpretation;
2. an observable result that a test could assert;
3. an implementation detail that should move to design.md; and
4. an assumption not supported by the decision table.
Do not rewrite the spec yet.
Do not treat that review as a replacement for a product owner, API owner, or developer. Use it to make ambiguities easier to see, then return each decision to the responsible person.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
text:
3.6 Validate structure, then review meaning
Run OpenSpec validation before handing the change to implementation:
openspec validate add-unit-number-search --strict
The validator can catch structural faults such as a requirement without a scenario. It cannot decide whether exact match means case-sensitive matching, whether an unknown unit number should produce an empty result, or whether the scenario reflects the Jira request. Treat a clean command as evidence that OpenSpec could parse the artifact, not as approval of its product meaning.
Use show when the parsed change needs inspection:
openspec show add-unit-number-search --json --deltas-only
Compare the parsed output with every intended requirement and scenario. If a heading level or section name prevents OpenSpec from recognizing one, fix the Markdown structure before continuing. Then return to human review for ambiguity, scope, and unsupported assumptions.

title: 3  Writing Requirements an Agent Can Test
section: 3.8 Maintain the requirement when behavior changes
text:
3.8 Maintain the requirement when behavior changes
Suppose a reviewed change resolves the earlier questions and the accepted specification now covers exact 15-character matching and no-match behavior. Later, another change would allow leading and trailing spaces around user input. Avoid appending a second, partly contradictory requirement. Use MODIFIED to restate the complete changed requirement and every scenario that should survive.
## MODIFIED Requirements

### Requirement: Search by unit number

The system SHALL ignore leading and trailing spaces around a search value and
match the remaining value against an exact 15-character unit number.

#### Scenario: Matching value surrounded by spaces

- **GIVEN** a truck exists with unit number `TRUCK-000001234`
- **WHEN** the user searches for `  TRUCK-000001234  `
- **THEN** the system returns that truck

#### Scenario: Matching unit number without surrounding spaces

- **GIVEN** a truck exists with unit number `TRUCK-000001234`
- **WHEN** the user searches for `TRUCK-000001234`
- **THEN** the system returns that truck

#### Scenario: No matching unit number

- **GIVEN** no truck has unit number `TRUCK-000009999`
- **WHEN** the user searches for `TRUCK-000009999`
- **THEN** the system returns no matching trucks
Restate the complete block because archive needs enough information to replace the accepted requirement without dropping scenarios that should remain. Match the existing requirement header exactly, then inspect the proposed difference with:
openspec show trim-unit-number-search --diff
Read that diff as a behavioral review. Confirm that the new wording changes only whitespace handling, that earlier scenarios remain, and that no implementation choice entered the contract. Resolve any discrepancy before archive updates the accepted spec.
Once the implementation and evidence satisfy the reviewed delta, archive can merge the change into openspec/specs/. The next agent can then read the current behavior without reconstructing it from old chats, Jira comments, or test names. Keep the archived change when the team needs the proposal, design discussion, and task history that explain how the requirement changed.

3.9 Hands-on exercise
Turn the unit-number Jira story into a reviewable OpenSpec delta:

Mark every ambiguous term in the story.
Create a decision table with Settled, Open, or Deferred for each question.
Draft one requirement using only settled decisions.

Ask an agent to find unsupported assumptions and implementation details.
Run openspec validate <change-name> --strict.
Map each scenario to expected test or runtime evidence.

Swap drafts with a partner. Could each of you derive the same observable behavior without agreeing on controller names, query methods, or component structure? Where your interpretations differ, revise the requirement or return the question to the decision table.

3.10 Verification checkpoint
Before calling the requirement ready, ask:

Can every normative term be traced to an accepted decision?
Could a reviewer observe each scenario’s result without reading private implementation details?
Does every requirement have at least one scenario that OpenSpec recognizes?
Do the scenarios cover the boundaries the team chose, rather than boundaries the agent invented?
Could the planned evidence fail when the specified behavior is wrong?
Would a future MODIFIED delta replace the requirement without losing behavior that should remain?

If one answer remains uncertain, keep the uncertainty visible. A short blocker costs less than a precise implementation of the wrong rule.

3.11 What you learned
Begin with decisions, not normative prose. Turn settled behavior into a requirement, use scenarios as observable examples, and let OpenSpec expose the proposed difference from the accepted baseline. Validate the structure, review the meaning, and trace each scenario to evidence before apply.
When behavior changes, revise the requirement through a complete delta and inspect what archive would carry forward. That maintenance step gives later agents a current contract rather than a pile of tests whose original intent must be guessed.

text:
4.1 Learning objective
Suppose you ask Copilot to add unit-number search to a Spring Boot service and its Angular client. You could attach the Jira story, both repositories, an architecture guide, several production logs, the OpenAPI document, and every test under src. Copilot would receive plenty of information, but the relevant constraints would be harder to find.
A smaller package might work better: the active OpenSpec change, the existing search endpoint, the generated-client boundary, and the commands that verify each repository. Let the agent search outward when those sources expose a gap. This approach treats context as a budget to allocate rather than a pile to maximize.
Build a bounded context package that preserves intent across a long-running change without crowding the selected model’s context window. Decide what belongs in repository instructions, OpenSpec artifacts, a chat session, or a Markdown handoff, then carry that package between VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA, and GitHub Copilot CLI.

4.2 Context engineering in an SDD workflow
Context engineering asks a practical question: what information should the model receive for this decision, in what form, and for how long? Prompt wording still matters, but the prompt forms only one part of the request. Copilot may also receive system instructions, repository customizations, conversation history, editor state, explicit file references, tool definitions, and tool output. VS Code documents this assembly process in its context guide1.
That larger definition fits SDD well. Instead of asking a chat transcript to remember the change, give each kind of information an owner:

Put facts that a future developer will need in an accepted spec, architecture record, or repository instruction. Keep implementation-specific facts in the active change or handoff. Evidence from one failed-test investigation can remain in chat unless the investigation must survive a session boundary.
This separation may feel slower than pasting everything into one prompt. It usually asks for more judgment at the beginning. In return, each new session can recover intent from named artifacts rather than from a transcript whose useful parts have become hard to distinguish from abandoned ideas.

section: 4.3 Treat the context window as shared space
text:
4.3 Treat the context window as shared space
A context window limits how much information a model can process in one request. Your current prompt does not get the whole window. System instructions, custom instructions, chat history, attached files, source snippets, tool schemas, terminal output, and space reserved for the response all compete for it.
More context can therefore make an answer worse. An obsolete design note might conflict with the accepted delta spec. A large log could push an earlier decision toward compaction. A folder attachment might bury the one validation rule that the implementation must preserve. Even relevant information has a cost when the model must repeatedly process it.
Evaluate each candidate source with four questions:

Does it affect the next decision or the requested output?
Is it more authoritative than another source already present?
Is it current, or could it describe behavior the team has replaced?
Could Copilot retrieve it later with a focused search instead of receiving it now?

Attach the source when the first three answers support it and retrieval would add avoidable uncertainty. Leave it discoverable when only a small part might become relevant. Remove or label it when its authority or freshness remains unclear.






WarningA large context window does not resolve contradictions



A model with room for both an old design and a new specification still has to choose between them. State which source wins, remove the stale source, or revise the artifacts before implementation.



4.3.1 Start with the smallest authoritative package
For the unit-number search change, an initial implementation request might include:

The active OpenSpec proposal, delta spec, design, and tasks.
The current controller or route that owns nearby search behavior.
The OpenAPI contract and the frontend service that consumes the generated client.
The narrow backend and frontend test commands.

Avoid attaching every controller, component, test, and generated client file. Ask the agent to inspect the named starting points and search for adjacent code before editing. VS Code’s semantic index can find relevant snippets without sending the entire workspace to every model request, while IntelliJ IDEA and Copilot CLI can use their own file references and agent tools to expand the working set as evidence requires.
A bounded request might read:
Implement the next unchecked task in the active add-unit-number-search change.
Treat its delta spec as the behavioral authority and design.md as the technical
boundary.  Start with the existing truck search endpoint and generated Angular
client.  Search for adjacent tests before editing.  Do not change generated files.
Run the narrow backend or frontend test named in tasks.md, then report the
scenario covered by the result.
Notice what this prompt does not repeat. It points to durable context instead of copying the requirements, architecture rules, and task list into chat. A correction to an artifact can then affect the next request without leaving a second version embedded in the transcript.

section: 4.4 Choose a model with the task and window in mind
text:
4.4 Choose a model with the task and window in mind
The selected model affects more than tone or coding style. Models may differ in context-window size, reasoning behavior, latency, supported inputs, and token price. VS Code’s context-window control reports the capacity available for the selected model, while Copilot CLI’s /model picker may offer a default or long-context tier for models that support one. GitHub’s model comparison2 changes as models enter and leave Copilot, so avoid encoding a permanent list of model names or limits in repository instructions.
A routine one-file edit rarely needs the largest available window. A faster model with focused context may finish at lower cost. An architecture review that compares both repositories, a contract, and competing designs may justify stronger reasoning and a larger window. Compare the total work required, including retries, rather than price or window size in isolation.
Before beginning a long task, select the model, context tier, reasoning effort, and tools you expect to use. Changing them later may alter available capacity, price, response behavior, or prompt-cache reuse. In VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA, use the model picker in the chat panel. In Copilot CLI, use /model; the picker can expose long-context options where the selected model supports them.
Keep two cautions in view:

A larger window may postpone compaction, but it may also invite an unfocused session and cost more per token.
A stronger reasoning model may complete a hard task with fewer retries, while the same model may waste credits on mechanical edits.

Use representative work from your repository to compare quality, retries, latency, and credit use. Recheck those results as Copilot’s model catalog and pricing change.

section: 4.5 Expect long conversations to be compacted
text:
4.5 Expect long conversations to be compacted
Conversation history cannot grow inside a fixed model window forever. As a session approaches its limit, Copilot can replace older turns with a shorter summary. That process, called context compaction, frees room for new prompts and tool results. It does not preserve every earlier sentence.
VS Code automatically compacts a conversation when its context window fills. You can inspect usage through the context-window control or run /compact before the limit, with guidance such as:
/compact Retain the accepted API contract, rejected persistence approaches,
failing test evidence, files changed, and the next unchecked OpenSpec task.
Copilot CLI also compacts automatically. Its current documentation describes background compaction as beginning near 80 percent of the token limit, with a dynamic threshold when static instructions and tool definitions already occupy much of the window. Use /context to inspect the window, /compact to request a focused summary, and /session checkpoints to inspect summaries created during the session. See the Copilot CLI context guidance3.
Do not treat automatic compaction as lossless memory. A summary may omit the reason an approach was rejected, the exact output of a failing test, or a small constraint mentioned many turns earlier. The chance of omission grows when the session mixes unrelated work.
Protect the state that must survive before compaction occurs:

Start a new session when the task changes.
Compact manually at a stable checkpoint rather than waiting for a crowded window.
Tell the compactor what must survive.
Move accepted facts into the artifact that owns them.
Save a reviewed handoff before closing or switching tools.

IntelliJ IDEA exposes chat history, file references, working sets, and plan handoff features, but its controls may not match VS Code or the CLI release for release. Keep durable context in repository files rather than depending on a client-specific transcript feature.

title: 4  Engineering Context for GitHub Copilot
section: 4.6 Carry the working state forward in Markdown
text:
4.6 Carry the working state forward in Markdown
A chat summary belongs to the chat system. A Markdown handoff belongs to the project and can be reviewed, diffed, attached to another session, or read from another client. Use one when an investigation or implementation will cross a session, model, developer, or IDE boundary.
Ask Copilot to draft the handoff, then verify every line against the repository and the active change. A useful file might look like this:
# Unit-number search handoff

Updated: 2026-09-21
Change: `add-unit-number-search`

## Current objective

Complete the backend search task without changing the accepted API contract.

## Sources of truth

- Behavior: `openspec/changes/add-unit-number-search/specs/vehicle-search/spec.md`
- Technical choices: `openspec/changes/add-unit-number-search/design.md`
- Remaining work: `openspec/changes/add-unit-number-search/tasks.md`

## Confirmed decisions

- Unit-number matching uses the rule stated in the delta spec.
- The backend owns the OpenAPI document.
- The Angular client remains generated code.

## Evidence

- `TruckSearchControllerTest` passes for the existing search path.
- The new no-match test fails because the repository query is not implemented.

## Rejected or superseded approaches

- Do not edit the generated TypeScript client by hand.
- Do not introduce a second search endpoint.

## Next action

Implement the repository query, run the focused backend test, and update the
matching checkbox in `tasks.md` only after the test passes.

## Open questions

- None for the current task.
Keep this file short. Link to specifications and source files instead of duplicating them. Record evidence with enough detail to reproduce it, and distinguish confirmed decisions from hypotheses. Delete the handoff when it no longer helps, or update it when the next developer would otherwise follow stale instructions.
A team might store the file at docs/handoffs/<change-name>.md, in a ticket-specific notes directory, or in another reviewed location outside generated output. Agree on one convention. If a handoff contains a lasting business rule, move that rule into the OpenSpec specification rather than allowing the handoff to become a shadow source of truth.
To start the next session, reference the handoff and the active change:
Read docs/handoffs/add-unit-number-search.md and the linked OpenSpec artifacts.
Verify that the handoff still matches the working tree and current test results.
Then perform only the Next action.  Stop and report any contradiction before
editing code.
That verification clause matters. A durable file can carry context forward, but durability also lets mistakes persist.

text:
4.7 Use each Copilot client deliberately
The same repository artifacts can support all three clients, while the attachment and inspection controls differ.

4.7.1 VS Code
VS Code can infer context from the active editor, selection, diagnostics, Git state, and workspace index. Use # mentions or Add Context when a file, folder, symbol, issue, pull request, terminal result, or URL must be considered. Attach a known source explicitly when omission would change the result; let workspace search discover ordinary neighboring code.
The context-window control can show current token use and the selected model’s capacity. Use /compact for a focused summary, /fork when exploring an alternative that should inherit the current history, and a new session for unrelated work. Check the response’s references when you need to confirm which instructions and files informed it.
Repository-wide rules may live in .github/copilot-instructions.md or AGENTS.md. Path-specific .instructions.md files can apply only to Java, TypeScript, tests, or selected folders. Keep always-on instructions short because they enter many requests. VS Code’s custom-instructions guide4 describes the current discovery rules.
Prompt files can still encode reusable requests for VS Code’s local agent, but current VS Code documentation marks them as deprecated for Agent Host sessions and recommends migration to Agent Skills. Prefer a skill for a reusable, multi-step workflow that should load only when relevant. Avoid moving change-specific requirements into a skill merely to make them reusable.


4.7.2 IntelliJ IDEA and other JetBrains IDEs
Copilot Chat in IntelliJ IDEA can use the open file or selected code as implicit context. Drag a file into the prompt, or right-click it and choose GitHub Copilot > Reference File in Chat, when the file must be part of the request. In edit mode, keep the working set limited to files the change may modify.
Use plan mode for a cross-cutting change, review the plan, and choose Open in Editor when you want the plan as Markdown. Save a reviewed version in the repository when it should outlive the conversation. The Copilot Chat guide for JetBrains IDEs5 covers file references, edit working sets, plan mode, and model selection.
Repository instructions can give VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Copilot CLI, and GitHub-hosted Copilot features a shared baseline, subject to each client’s current support. Inspect the response references instead of assuming an instruction file loaded. Avoid placing client-specific button sequences in repository-wide coding rules.


4.7.3 GitHub Copilot CLI
Start Copilot CLI from the narrowest directory that owns the task. Add a file with @relative/path, inspect context use with /context, and check model and token statistics with /usage. Use /new when changing topics and /compact <focus> when the current task should continue with less history.
The CLI can resume sessions, but a resumed transcript still carries its earlier assumptions and compacted summaries. A checked-in handoff and OpenSpec change may provide a cleaner restart than an old conversation. Use /share file when you need a Markdown export of the session, then distill the useful facts rather than treating the full transcript as project documentation.
Use /instructions to inspect discovered instruction files. Keep @file references focused, and consider subagents for isolated exploration because each subagent has a separate context window and can return a concise result to the main session. The Copilot CLI command reference6 documents these commands and the current model options.

section: 4.8 Understand caching without confusing it with memory
text:
4.8 Understand caching without confusing it with memory
Prompt caching may let a model provider reuse an unchanged prefix from a previous request. That prefix can include stable system instructions, tool definitions, custom instructions, and earlier conversation content. When supported by the provider and model, reuse may lower latency and the cost assigned to cached input tokens.
Caching does not enlarge the context window. It does not guarantee that Copilot will recall an omitted fact. It also does not replace compaction or a handoff file. The same tokens may remain part of the model request even when the provider can process them at a lower cached-input rate.
GitHub’s current token-based pricing converts input, output, cache-read, and, for some models, cache-write tokens into GitHub AI Credits. The rates vary by model, and one AI credit represents $0.01 USD under that billing model. Some annual plans may still use legacy request-based billing, so check the plan that applies to your account. See Models and pricing for GitHub Copilot7.
To improve cache reuse without weakening the request, choose the model, reasoning effort, context tier, instructions, and tool set before the session begins. Keep stable instructions stable. Avoid repeatedly replacing large attachments or changing the tool catalog between turns without a task-related reason. Forking an existing VS Code session may preserve the earlier prompt prefix better than reconstructing it in a new chat.
Do not optimize a cache-hit percentage at the expense of correctness. A changed specification should invalidate the old context. A required MCP tool should remain available even if its schema changes the prompt prefix. VS Code’s Cache Explorer8 can show where consecutive requests first diverge, but the documentation cautions that this comparison does not prove how the provider processed or billed the request.

section: 4.9 Reduce context waste before it reaches the model
text:
4.9 Reduce context waste before it reaches the model
Several small practices can keep the useful signal easier to recover:

Give each session one change or investigation.
Attach a precise file or symbol before attaching a folder or codebase.
Exclude generated output, dependencies, build directories, and noisy logs from search when they should not be discovered.
Keep tool catalogs narrow; every tool definition and result may consume context.
Run deterministic bulk work in a script or build tool, then return the concise result instead of many repetitive tool calls.
Use a subagent for independent research and ask for a sourced summary.
Ask Copilot to name the files, instructions, assumptions, and test evidence behind a recommendation.
Correct the owning artifact when a rule changes rather than repeating the correction in later prompts.
Start a fresh session when the accumulated history costs more than rebuilding a small context package.

MCP servers can supply current data from issue trackers, documentation systems, or internal services. Add one when the task needs information that the repository cannot contain or should not duplicate. Limit enabled servers and tools to the current job; a large catalog consumes context before any tool runs and gives the agent more choices to evaluate.
The same restraint applies to custom instructions. A linter can enforce formatting without spending context tokens on a prose rule. Source code can reveal an ordinary framework convention. Reserve instructions for non-obvious constraints, commands, boundaries, and exceptions that Copilot would otherwise have to rediscover or might infer incorrectly.

4.10 Hands-on exercise
Take one oversized prompt from your work or use the unit-number search example. Break it into these layers:

Move stable repository facts into .github/copilot-instructions.md or a path-specific instruction file.
Move accepted and proposed behavior into the appropriate OpenSpec artifacts.
Keep the current objective and evidence in a focused session.
Attach only the files needed to begin, then let the agent search for adjacent code.
Ask Copilot to draft a Markdown handoff using the template in this chapter.
Review the handoff against the working tree, test output, and active OpenSpec change.
Start a fresh session in another client and reference only the handoff and its linked artifacts.

Ask the new session to state the current objective, authoritative sources, next action, and unresolved questions before editing. If it cannot recover those facts without the old transcript, revise the durable artifacts or handoff rather than pasting the transcript into the new session.
For a second pass, compare a focused and an overloaded run of the same bounded task. Record the selected model, context use, tool calls, AI credits, retries, and verification result. One run will not establish a universal rule, but it may expose noisy sources or missing instructions in your repository.

title: 4  Engineering Context for GitHub Copilot
text:
4.11 Verification checkpoint
Before handing implementation to Copilot, ask:

Does the session have one bounded objective and an observable completion condition?
Can every attached source affect the next decision?
Does each rule have one named owner, with stale or conflicting copies removed?
Could the selected model hold the required context with room for tools and output?
Have accepted decisions moved out of chat and into a durable artifact?
Would automatic compaction be allowed to omit anything that has not been saved?
Can another client recover the objective from the repository without the old transcript?
Did you inspect references, tests, and usage rather than infer that context was applied?

An uncertain answer may call for a smaller task, a better artifact, or a new session. Adding the whole repository rarely resolves that uncertainty.

title: 4  Engineering Context for GitHub Copilot
text:
4.12 What you learned
Treat context as a bounded input to each model request. Keep stable rules in repository instructions, proposed behavior in OpenSpec, reusable procedures in skills, and short-lived evidence in a focused session. Before a session boundary, move verified working state into a reviewed Markdown handoff.
Model choice changes the available window, behavior, and price. Compaction summarizes rather than preserving every detail, and caching reduces processing cost rather than creating memory. Give Copilot the smallest current, authoritative package from which it can complete and verify the next task.

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.1 Learning objective
The exercises in Part II use two prepared repositories: commercial-truck-search-api and commercial-truck-search-ui. Although they support one product, each repository will keep its own openspec/ folder, accepted specifications, active changes, and archive.
A backend change and a frontend change may support the same user capability without making the same decisions. In this lab, the backend owns API behavior and the OpenAPI contract. The frontend owns the user’s interaction with that contract and consumes a generated TypeScript Angular client. This arrangement keeps each specification beside the code that can enforce and test it.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to explain why each repository has a separate OpenSpec project, trace a full-stack change across the contract boundary, and establish a working baseline for both repositories. Your baseline should record the tool versions, application ports, verification commands, and clean commits needed to repeat the later exercises.

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
text:
5.2 One product, two specification histories
After initialization in the next chapter, the repositories should have parallel OpenSpec structures. A simplified view might look like this:
commercial-truck-search-api/
|-- openspec/
|   |-- specs/
|   `-- changes/
|       `-- archive/
|-- src/
`-- ...

commercial-truck-search-ui/
|-- openspec/
|   |-- specs/
|   `-- changes/
|       `-- archive/
|-- src/
`-- ...
The matching folder names do not imply shared contents. In the backend repository, openspec/specs/ may describe accepted API behavior such as valid search input, response shapes, and error semantics. In the frontend repository, the same path may describe accepted user behavior such as form validation, loading feedback, result presentation, and empty or error states.
Each openspec/changes/ directory can hold work for its repository. A backend change may include tasks for a controller, service, persistence query, tests, and OpenAPI publication. Its frontend counterpart may include tasks for a form, generated-client integration, view states, and browser tests. Neither change needs to carry the other’s implementation plan.
Two change folders can drift in names, assumptions, or timing. Explicit ownership and a recorded dependency can expose that drift without copying the same requirement into both repositories.

title: 5  Preparing the Two-Repository Lab
section: 5.3 Let the contract cross the boundary
text:
5.3 Let the contract cross the boundary
For the later unit-number search, the work might move through the repositories in this order:

Explore the user capability across both repositories.
Create linked backend and frontend OpenSpec changes.
Let the backend change define the observable API behavior and OpenAPI contract.
Let the frontend change define the user interaction and record its contract dependency.
Implement and test the backend, then publish the reviewed OpenAPI document.
Generate the TypeScript client, then implement and test the frontend behavior.

This order leaves one owner for the wire contract while allowing both proposals to be reviewed before implementation. The frontend specification can define the user experience and record its dependency without restating endpoint fields by hand. If the frontend needs a field or error response that the contract does not provide, the team can revise the backend change before client generation.
The relationship may be easier to remember as a dependency:
linked OpenSpec changes
  |
  v
backend implementation and reviewed OpenAPI contract
  |
  v
generated TypeScript Angular client
  |
  v
frontend implementation
Frontend exploration may expose a missing API decision before implementation begins. The team can then resolve that decision in the backend change and regenerate the client instead of editing generated TypeScript or creating a competing frontend definition.

5.4 Decide where a statement belongs
When a requirement touches both repositories, ask which codebase can verify and enforce it. The answer may prevent a shared idea from becoming two independent rules.








Statement
OpenSpec owner
Reason




Which unit-number inputs the API accepts
Backend
The API validates the request boundary


Which status and body represent no match
Backend
The OpenAPI contract exposes this behavior


When the search control becomes available
Frontend
The UI owns the interaction


What the user sees while a request runs
Frontend

Which response fields the generated client exposes
Backend
The backend publishes the schema


How response fields appear on the page
Frontend
The UI owns presentation



Some scenarios may need evidence in both repositories. Invalid input, for example, could have a backend scenario for API enforcement and a frontend scenario for immediate feedback. Each scenario can use the agreed meaning of valid input while describing behavior that its own repository can test.






WarningAvoid a third source of truth



A cross-repository planning note can link the two changes and record their order. It should not become another specification of request fields, response codes, or UI behavior. Put each lasting rule in the OpenSpec project that owns it, and let the OpenAPI document carry the wire contract.

Separate histories help only when you can tell what each change introduced. Before initializing OpenSpec or asking Copilot to implement a feature, establish a baseline in both repositories. A failed build at this point may indicate a toolchain or checkout problem. The same failure after a change may indicate a regression. Without the baseline, the two explanations can be difficult to separate.

Later chapters use its absence as the starting condition for the first feature.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.1 Learning objective
Running openspec init takes little time. The harder part is deciding what the generated setup needs to teach an agent about the repository.
Initialization places the OpenSpec project beside the code it describes and installs workflow files for the selected AI tool. Configuration supplies the repository context used by those workflows. Keeping these steps separate distinguishes generated OpenSpec guidance from rules the team owns.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to initialize OpenSpec for GitHub Copilot, explain which files the CLI generates, and configure each lab repository with concise planning context. You will also review the resulting diff and decide whether the repository is ready for the exploration workflow in Chapter 7.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.2 Begin at the repository root
Chapter 5 established a clean baseline for commercial-truck-search-api and commercial-truck-search-ui. Because initialization writes files into the current project, that baseline provides the comparison point for the changes that follow. Running the command from a parent directory or the wrong terminal risks initializing the wrong folder.
Before changing either repository, inspect the working directory and Git state:
pwd
git status --short
Does the path identify the root of one lab repository? Does an empty git status --short result match the baseline from Chapter 5? If either answer is no, stop before running initialization.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.3 Separate installation from initialization
Install the OpenSpec CLI once on the machine, then initialize each repository separately. The global installation can support both lab repositories, but each repository needs its own OpenSpec project and Copilot integration files.
For the book’s pinned version, install the package and check the executable:
npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@1.13.1
openspec --version
The second command needs to report 1.13.1 for the exercises in this book. If another version appears, resolve the mismatch before generating files because CLI versions can install different workflow content. The installation appendix covers operating-system-specific installation and PATH checks.






NoteA profile is not a technology stack



The core profile selects the standard OpenSpec workflows, such as explore, propose, apply, update, sync, and archive. It does not describe Java, Spring Boot, Angular, or the test tools in a repository. Put those project facts in openspec/config.yaml after initialization.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.4 What initialization adds
From a repository root, the following command selects GitHub Copilot without opening the interactive tool picker:
openspec init --tools github-copilot --profile core
OpenSpec creates an openspec/ directory and installs Copilot workflow files under .github/. The workflow count depends on the selected profile and OpenSpec version, so review the command summary rather than assuming a fixed count.
A newly initialized repository resembles this simplified tree:
repository-root/
|-- .github/
|   |-- prompts/
|   `-- skills/
|-- openspec/
|   |-- config.yaml
|   |-- specs/
|   `-- changes/
|       `-- archive/
`-- ...
The directories have different jobs:








Path
Intended role
Review question




openspec/config.yaml
Repository context, artifact rules, and operation guidance
Does this describe this repository rather than the whole product?


openspec/specs/
Accepted behavior after changes have been archived or synchronized
Is it empty for this new baseline?


openspec/changes/
Proposed work that has not yet entered the accepted specifications
Is it empty before Chapter 8?


.github/skills/
OpenSpec workflows GitHub Copilot may select as skills
Did initialization install the expected workflow set?


.github/prompts/
Prompt files exposed by supported Copilot IDE integrations
Does the IDE discover them after a restart?



Do not use initialization to invent accepted product behavior. Empty specs/ and changes/ directories are the expected result for these lab repositories. Later chapters add content through reviewed changes.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
section: 6.5 Configure context that can affect every change
text:
6.5 Configure context that can affect every change
OpenSpec reads openspec/config.yaml when a workflow asks the CLI for artifact or operation instructions. The context field reaches proposal, specification, design, task, apply, and archive work. Reserve it for facts that belong in every one of those prompts.
Useful context answers questions that source inspection alone may not settle:

Which repository boundary does this project own?
Which contract does it publish or consume?
Which verification commands should planned work include?
Which generated files should an agent avoid editing by hand?
Which architectural or product constraints should shape every change?

Avoid turning config.yaml into a second README. File locations that an agent can discover, temporary implementation details, and lengthy style guides consume context without improving a plan. Prefer a short repository-specific rule to a page of general advice.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.6 Configure the backend repository
Use the backend OpenSpec project to describe the boundary owned by commercial-truck-search-api. Its context identifies the service stack, the OpenAPI ownership rule, and the checks required before a task is complete.
After initialization, revise openspec/config.yaml toward a compact form such as this:
schema: spec-driven

context: |
  Repository: commercial-truck-search-api
  Tech stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1, Maven, Spring Data JPA, and H2.
  This repository owns API behavior and the reviewed OpenAPI contract.
  Backend changes should preserve the existing controller, service, and persistence boundaries.

rules:
  specs:
    - Describe observable API behavior without prescribing Java implementation details.
    - Include scenarios for validation, successful results, no match, and relevant errors.
  tasks:
    - Include automated tests and OpenAPI publication when a contract changes.

operations:
  apply:
    guidance:
      - Run the repository's Maven tests before marking implementation tasks complete.
Treat this example as a starting point, not verified repository configuration. Confirm every version, command, and ownership statement against the Chapter 5 baseline before committing it. If the repository uses a Maven wrapper, name that checked-in command rather than a machine-wide Maven executable.
Notice what the example leaves out. Frontend rendering rules do not belong here, and the future unit-number endpoint has not yet been specified. Configuration can establish planning boundaries without deciding the behavior of a change that the team has not explored.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.7 Configure the frontend repository
The frontend project needs different context because it owns user interaction and consumes the generated TypeScript client. Copying the backend configuration would give Copilot the wrong ownership model even though both repositories support the same product.
A starting configuration could look like this:
schema: spec-driven

context: |
  Repository: commercial-truck-search-ui
  Tech stack: Angular 21, TypeScript, Vitest, component tests, and Playwright.
  This repository owns user interaction and consumes a generated TypeScript API client.
  Do not edit generated client files by hand or redefine the backend wire contract here.

rules:
  specs:
    - Describe user-visible behavior, including loading, empty, validation, and error states.
    - Refer to the backend contract as a dependency rather than duplicating its schema.
  tasks:
    - Include the appropriate unit, component, or browser test for each behavior change.

operations:
  apply:
    guidance:
      - Run the repository's configured frontend tests before marking tasks complete.
This configuration should not make the generated client a source of product decisions. The backend owns the OpenAPI contract, while the frontend can record how it uses that contract and how the browser should respond to each state. If a frontend proposal needs a response field that the contract does not provide, the missing field should return to the backend change for review.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
section: 6.8 Understand generated files and team-owned context
text:
6.8 Understand generated files and team-owned context
The workflow files under .github/ come from the installed OpenSpec package. Review and commit them, but avoid hand-editing generated instructions. A later openspec update could replace or conflict with local edits.
The repository context in openspec/config.yaml carries a different responsibility. OpenSpec creates the file, but the team supplies and reviews the facts inside it. Divide ownership this way:








Material
Primary source
Maintenance action




Workflow instructions and prompt files
Installed OpenSpec package
Refresh with openspec update


Workflow selection and delivery preference
OpenSpec profile on the developer machine
Change the profile, then update each repository


Repository planning context and rules
Repository team
Edit and review openspec/config.yaml


Accepted behavior and active changes
Product and engineering review
Change through the OpenSpec workflow



This distinction prevents two common mistakes: placing repository architecture in generated prompt files and expecting a global profile to describe a particular codebase.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
section: 6.9 Review initialization as a code change
text:
6.9 Review initialization as a code change
Initialization deserves the same diff review as any other repository-wide tool addition. Because plain git diff omits untracked files, stage the generated files before reviewing their content:
git status --short
git add openspec '.github/skills/openspec-*' '.github/prompts/opsx-*.prompt.md'
git diff --cached -- openspec '.github/skills/openspec-*' '.github/prompts/opsx-*.prompt.md'
During review, ask:

Did OpenSpec write into the intended repository root?
Does openspec/config.yaml name only facts that apply to this repository?
Do backend rules stay out of the frontend project, and vice versa?
Are accepted specifications and active changes still empty at this stage?
Did initialization overwrite an existing team-owned Copilot file?
Can another developer understand which files come from OpenSpec and which context the team must maintain?

Re-running openspec init refreshes files in an initialized project, but still review the diff. When an installed CLI or profile changes, use the direct maintenance command:
openspec update
The update command refreshes configured workflow files from the installed CLI. Review those changes before committing them, especially when the team changes the pinned OpenSpec version.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.10 Verify the initialized repositories
Run the following checks from each repository root:
openspec --version
openspec doctor
openspec list --specs
openspec list
git status --short
At this point in the lab, expect version 1.13.1, a health report with the intended OpenSpec root, no accepted specifications, and no active changes. The Git output should list only the initialization and configuration files you intend to commit.
openspec validate --all checks discovered changes and specifications, but an empty project has no such artifacts yet. A successful empty validation confirms only that OpenSpec found no invalid item. It does not verify the accuracy of the repository context; reviewers must do that.
Restart VS Code or IntelliJ IDEA after initialization so the IDE can discover newly installed Copilot prompt files. Then confirm that the expected OpenSpec workflows appear in Copilot Chat. If the terminal commands work but the chat entries do not appear, investigate IDE discovery before changing the OpenSpec project structure.

title: 6  Initialize and Configure OpenSpec
text:
6.11 Hands-on exercise: initialize both repositories

Confirm the repository root and clean baseline.
Verify that the CLI reports version 1.13.1.

Run the verification commands and restart the IDE.
Commit each repository’s initialization separately so later feature changes have a clean boundary.

Compare the two config.yaml files before committing. Their shared schema and workflow look similar, but their ownership statements, testing guidance, and generated-code boundaries are not interchangeable.
