title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.1 Learning objective
A Jira story asks for search by a 15-character unit number. That sentence may be enough to name the feature, but would it be enough to write the first test? Does “15-character” describe the stored value or the text a user may enter? Would a valid number with no matching truck produce an empty result, a 404, or a message on the page? Which repository would own each answer?
OpenSpec exploration can keep those questions visible while the team examines the request and the two repositories. The work in this chapter stops before proposal artifacts or code, when the team can tell which behavior has evidence and which behavior still needs a decision.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to explore the unit-number search without silently designing it. Your output should be a reviewable decision record that separates facts from inferences, names unresolved questions, and assigns an owner or next action to each question.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.2 Treat exploration as investigation
What should exploration produce? Not proposal.md, design.md, or tasks.md. Those artifacts would ask the team to review behavior that may still be in dispute. The immediate output should be a record of what the story states, what the repositories demonstrate, and what neither source can decide.
Consider the cost of skipping that separation. A backend agent could infer exact matching and return 404 for no result, while a frontend agent could infer partial matching and expect an empty list. Each implementation might look reasonable in its own repository. The generated client and the page would still expose the disagreement.
Exploration should therefore move from the story to repository evidence, then route unanswered questions to an owner. The reviewed record, rather than the chat transcript, could then become the source for the proposal in Chapter 8.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.3 Begin with the thin request
For this exercise, begin with the available statement:

Users need to search for a commercial truck by its 15-character unit number.

What can that sentence support on its own? It names a user goal, an entity, a search field, and a length. Everything else in the table below would need evidence or a decision.
A first pass could classify the story this way:








Statement
Classification
What it permits




Users search for a commercial truck
Stated intent
Scope a truck-search capability


Search uses a unit number
Stated intent
Investigate that field across both repositories


The unit number has 15 characters
Stated constraint
Ask where and how length is validated


Matching is exact
Unstated
Raise a question; do not write a requirement


Lowercase input is accepted
Unstated
Inspect normalization behavior, then ask if needed


No match returns 404
Unstated
Compare API conventions without selecting one



The last three rows might sound reasonable, but the story does not support them. Repository precedent could make one of them a sensible option; only review could turn that option into accepted behavior.
Keep the Jira identifier and its exact wording with the exploration record. That link could later let reviewers trace an OpenSpec proposal back to its business source without asking the issue to carry details it never contained.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.4 Establish the exploration boundary
Before opening Copilot Chat, decide what the agent may inspect and what it should leave untouched. For the two-repository lab, the useful boundary would include:

the backend controllers, services, persistence queries, validation, error responses, tests, and reviewed OpenAPI contract;
the frontend search forms, generated-client usage, loading and error states, result views, and tests;
each repository’s openspec/config.yaml and relevant Copilot instructions; and
the Jira story or a faithful excerpt supplied in the prompt.

A generated TypeScript client may reveal the current API contract, but it should not decide what a new endpoint ought to return. Old chat messages deserve the same caution unless their claims can be traced to the story, the current repository baseline, or a recorded team decision.






Warning



Exploration can expose a missing decision, but it cannot approve that decision. When repository evidence conflicts with the Jira story, keep the conflict visible and send it to the person who owns the behavior.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
section: 7.5 Ask Copilot for evidence, not a solution
text:
7.5 Ask Copilot for evidence, not a solution
Open the backend repository in the IDE, start the OpenSpec exploration workflow, and supply the story as quoted source material. A prompt such as the following could constrain the response:
/opsx:explore We are considering an initial commercial-truck search capability:
"Users need to search for a commercial truck by its 15-character unit number."

Investigate this request without creating a proposal, specification, design, tasks, or code.
Inspect the current repository and report:

1. Relevant existing routes, domain fields, validation, error handling, persistence queries,
     tests, and OpenAPI conventions.
2. What the Jira statement explicitly requires.
3. Candidate behavior suggested by repository evidence, with file references.
4. Questions the repository cannot answer, including exact versus partial matching,
     normalization, malformed input, no-match behavior, response fields, and non-goals.
5. A decision-record table with columns for question, evidence, status, owner, and next action.

Label every item as Stated, Observed, Inferred, or Open.  Do not convert an inference into a
requirement.
Why ask for file references? Without them, “the repository validates identifiers this way” may be no more than a fluent guess. A controller, schema, test, or generated contract gives the reviewer something to inspect. When Copilot cannot cite evidence, the item should remain inferred or open.
Run a corresponding exploration in the frontend repository. Adjust the first list so the agent looks for form controls, validators, generated-client calls, visible states, and interaction tests. Keep the same source labels and decision-record columns so the two reports can be compared without first rewriting them into a common shape.
crumbs: Part II: Establishing the Greenfield Baseline
7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.6 Separate evidence from inference
An exploration response may mix four kinds of material in one polished paragraph. Give each claim one of these labels before using it:








Label
Meaning
Suitable next use




Stated
The Jira story says it directly
Candidate scope or constraint


Observed
A cited repository artifact demonstrates it
Evidence for a convention or dependency


Inferred
The agent connects stated intent with observed precedent
Option for review, not accepted behavior


Open
Neither the story nor repository settles it
Owner decision or explicit deferral



Suppose the agent finds an existing identifier search that trims whitespace. The finding would be observed behavior for that endpoint. Applying the same rule to unit numbers would remain an inference until the team accepts it.
Check each cited file and ask a few direct questions:

Does the cited code execute in the current search path, or is it unused or generated?
Does a test demonstrate behavior, or merely arrange test data?
Does the OpenAPI document describe the implemented contract at the pinned baseline?
Does the evidence belong to this repository, or did the agent import a convention from the other project?
Did the response answer a business question by choosing the easiest implementation?

If a citation fails one of those checks, change the claim from “Observed” to “Inferred” or “Open.”

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
text:
7.7 Build one cross-repository question set
The backend and frontend reports will probably overlap without matching exactly. Merge them by question rather than by prose. The resulting question set might look like this:








Question
Why implementation depends on it
Likely owner




Must all 15 characters match?
Determines query semantics and UI expectations
Product owner


May input contain spaces, hyphens, or lowercase letters?
Determines normalization and validation
Product owner with backend lead


What happens for empty or malformed input?
Shapes API errors and immediate form feedback
Product owner with API and UI leads


What happens when no truck matches?
Must agree across HTTP response, client behavior, and page state
API and UI leads


Which truck fields appear in a successful result?
Defines the backend-owned response contract
Product owner with backend lead


May more than one truck match?
Determines whether the response is an object or collection
Product owner


Which searches remain out of scope?
Prevents VIN, partial, and multi-field search from entering the change
Product owner



“Likely owner” should remain a routing suggestion until the team confirms it. The agent can show who appears to own an existing contract or component, but organizational authority may not be visible in either repository.

title: 7  Exploring the Unit-Number Search
section: 7.8 Turn questions into a decision record
text:
7.8 Turn questions into a decision record
Build the decision record from the merged question set. Each row should preserve the evidence reviewed, the current status, the owner, and the next action; an open cell should not be filled with a guess merely to make the table look complete.
| Question | Evidence | Status | Owner | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exact or partial match? | Jira gives only field and length | Open | Product owner | Choose match semantics |
| Normalize input? | Existing endpoint trims input at `path:line` | Inferred option | Product owner + backend lead | Confirm whether precedent applies |
| Malformed input? | API uses validation response at `path:line` | Candidate convention | Backend lead | Propose error shape after product decision |
| No matching truck? | Backend and UI precedents differ | Open conflict | API + UI leads | Agree on one cross-repository behavior |
| Result fields? | Current truck summary type at `path:line` | Inferred option | Product owner | Approve fields or request a smaller projection |
| VIN search? | Not named in Jira | Deferred non-goal | Product owner | Confirm exclusion from first change |
Replace each path:line placeholder with a real repository reference during the lab. If no reference supports a row, mark the evidence as unavailable.
Notice the difference between “Open” and “Deferred non-goal.” An open question blocks some part of the proposed behavior. A deferred item has an explicit boundary and may be considered in a later change. Calling an unanswered question “out of scope” would hide a decision rather than postpone it responsibly.

text:
8.1 Learning objective
Chapter 7 ended with a decision record, not a plan. How might that record become a change that a backend developer, a frontend developer, and Copilot could inspect without replaying the original conversation? Which decisions belong in shared behavior, which belong to one repository, and which should still block implementation?
Follow the unit-number search through OpenSpec’s proposal workflow. Keep the backend and frontend work in separate active changes, then connect them through one reviewed API contract and an explicit handoff. Aim for more than a set of completed Markdown files: give reviewers a cheap way to find scope drift before either repository changes application code.
Use this chapter to turn a reviewed exploration record into proposal, delta specification, design, and task artifacts for a full-stack capability. By the end, you should be able to explain why two repository changes are preferable here, trace a scenario across both changes, and decide whether the pair is ready for the apply workflow.

text:
8.2 Treat proposal as a review boundary
Do not treat entry into the proposal workflow as evidence that behavior has shipped. Treat it as the point where the team places a specific difference under review while the accepted product behavior remains unchanged.
That distinction should affect how you read the generated files:








Artifact
Question for the reviewer
Warning sign




proposal.md
Why should this change exist, and where should it stop?
Classes, methods, or response details appear before the scope has been accepted


specs/<capability>/spec.md
What new behavior could a user or client observe?
A scenario depends on an unanswered question or names implementation machinery


design.md
How might this repository satisfy the behavior?
A technical choice quietly creates new user-visible behavior


tasks.md
What work and evidence would complete the change?
A task has no requirement, or a requirement has no implementation and verification task



Use one proposal when the affected code and review path belong to one repository. For this lab, keep one active change in each repository because the applications have separate code, tests, and ownership boundaries. Connect those changes through the contract dependency instead of hiding the boundary inside one plan.
Before generating files, trace one accepted decision through the artifacts it would affect:
accepted no-match decision
      |
      +-- backend scenario
      |     +-- response-mapping design decision
      |     `-- API test task
      |
      `-- frontend empty-state scenario
          +-- state-handling design decision
          `-- component test task
Use the same trace for valid input, a successful match, and each reviewed error. A broken branch would expose a missing artifact before implementation begins.

text:
8.3 Check whether exploration is ready to become a proposal
Before invoking the proposal workflow, reopen the Chapter 7 decision record. Ask whether a reviewer could write an observable scenario without supplying another assumption.
Use questions such as these:

Has the product owner selected exact or partial matching?
Has the team agreed on valid input, normalization, and no-match behavior?
Has someone approved the fields returned for a match?
Have related searches, such as VIN or multi-field search, been accepted or deferred?
Does each unresolved item have an owner and a reason it does not block this change?

Do not mistake an assigned owner for permission to ignore a blocking question. If the answer could change a response status, request constraint, result shape, or visible UI state, pause the proposal and get the decision. If the answer affects only a later capability, record the deferral and keep it outside the current scope.






WarningDo not let the example choose the product behavior



The artifact excerpts below illustrate structure. Replace bracketed text with the reviewed decisions from your Chapter 7 record. Do not treat exact matching, an empty result, or any example response shape as accepted merely because it appears in this chapter.

8.4 Name two changes around one capability
Choose names that describe outcomes rather than layers or ticket numbers. For the lab, the two change directories might look like this:
commercial-truck-search-api/
`-- openspec/changes/add-unit-number-search-api/
    |-- proposal.md
    |-- specs/unit-number-search/spec.md
    |-- design.md
    `-- tasks.md

commercial-truck-search-ui/
`-- openspec/changes/add-unit-number-search-ui/
    |-- proposal.md
    |-- specs/unit-number-search/spec.md
    |-- design.md
    `-- tasks.md
Use repository-qualified names when they make cross-repository review notes and build output easier to read. The suffix matters less than using the same capability term, unit-number-search, in both delta specifications.
Record the ownership boundary before asking Copilot to draft either change:








Concern
Backend change
Frontend change




Accepted search rule
Express API-observable behavior
Refer to the same rule through user-visible interaction


Wire contract
Own and publish the reviewed OpenAPI document
Consume a generated client from that document


Validation
Enforce the API boundary
Offer immediate feedback without weakening or redefining the API rule


Outcomes
Return the reviewed success, no-match, and error responses
Render loading, result, empty, and error states


Verification
Test service and HTTP behavior; inspect the contract
Test interaction and rendering; exercise the generated client boundary

title: 8  Proposing the First Full-Stack Change
text:
8.5 Draft the backend change first
Start in the backend repository because its reviewed contract constrains the frontend handoff. In Copilot Chat, adapt the following prompt to the decisions you actually recorded:
/opsx:propose add-unit-number-search-api

Using the attached Chapter 7 decision record, draft an OpenSpec change for the backend-owned
unit-number search capability.

Please:
- treat only Accepted decisions as requirements;
- preserve Open and Deferred items as dependencies or non-goals;
- keep Java, Spring, persistence, and controller choices out of behavioral requirements;
- include scenarios for each accepted valid-input, match, no-match, and invalid-input outcome;
- record OpenAPI publication and backend verification in the design and tasks; and
- stop and report any decision needed to write an observable scenario.

Do not modify application code or accepted specs.
After generation, inspect the artifact order rather than accepting the folder as one indivisible answer. The proposal should constrain the delta and design; the delta and design should constrain the task list.

8.5.1 Read proposal.md for scope
A compact backend proposal might use this shape:
# Change: Add unit-number search API

## Why

Fleet coordinators need to locate a commercial truck from the unit number supplied in their
workflow.

## What Changes

- Add API behavior for searching by a [reviewed valid unit-number rule].
- Return the [reviewed match and no-match outcomes].
- Publish the request, response, and error behavior in OpenAPI.

## Non-Goals

- VIN search
- Partial or multi-field search
- Frontend rendering behavior

## Dependencies

- The frontend change may generate its client only after review of the published OpenAPI document.
Review the proposal before reading its dependent artifacts:

Does Why justify the work without restating the Jira title?
Does What Changes name observable scope without selecting endpoint classes or query methods?
Do the non-goals prevent plausible but unwanted expansion?

Revise the proposal first if any answer is no.


8.5.2 Read the backend delta for behavior
Insert the approved input, result, and error decisions into the delta. Until then, keep explicit placeholders rather than completing the requirement from repository precedent or convention:
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Search by unit number

The API SHALL accept a unit number that satisfies [the reviewed input rule] and return
[the reviewed result shape].

#### Scenario: Matching truck exists

- **WHEN** a client searches with a valid unit number that matches a truck
- **THEN** the API returns the reviewed truck representation

#### Scenario: No matching truck exists

- **WHEN** a client searches with a valid unit number that matches no truck
- **THEN** the API returns the reviewed no-match response

#### Scenario: Unit number is invalid

- **WHEN** a client searches with a unit number that violates the reviewed input rule
- **THEN** the API returns the reviewed validation response
Check whether each scenario could become an HTTP-level test without knowledge of a Java class. Keep invalid input distinct from valid input with no match, and map every placeholder to an accepted row in the decision record. Leave a missing answer visible rather than replacing it with whatever behavior seems conventional.


8.5.3 Read design.md for consequential choices
Now ask how the backend might satisfy those scenarios. A useful design would usually discuss the request boundary, service and persistence path, error mapping, OpenAPI publication, and test levels. It might record a decision in this form:
## Decision: Publish the backend contract before client generation

Generate the OpenAPI document from the implemented backend boundary and review it against the
delta scenarios before the frontend generates a client.

### Rationale

This order keeps request constraints, result fields, and error responses under backend ownership.

### Consequence

The frontend implementation task remains blocked until the reviewed contract artifact is
available.
Apply a replacement test to each statement. If swapping Spring Data for another persistence mechanism would preserve the statement, keep the mechanism in the design. If changing case handling would alter what a client observes, place that rule in the delta rather than hiding it in a mapper or query decision.

section: 8.6 Draft the frontend change from the contract boundary
text:
8.6 Draft the frontend change from the contract boundary
Create the frontend proposal only after the backend scope and observable contract have survived review. The OpenAPI document need not exist yet, but the dependency and ownership rule should.
/opsx:propose add-unit-number-search-ui

Using the reviewed backend change and the attached Chapter 7 decision record, draft an OpenSpec
change for the Angular unit-number search interaction.

Please:
- describe user-visible input, loading, result, empty, validation, and error behavior;
- refer to the backend-owned OpenAPI contract instead of duplicating request or response schemas;
- make client generation depend on the reviewed backend contract;
- keep Angular component and service choices in design.md; and
- include tests and a cross-application verification task.

Do not edit generated client files or application code.
Write the frontend scenarios from the user’s interaction rather than restating HTTP mechanics. A representative excerpt might read:
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Search for a truck by unit number

The interface SHALL let a user submit a unit number that satisfies [the reviewed input rule].

#### Scenario: Search is in progress

- **WHEN** the user submits a valid unit number and the request has not completed
- **THEN** the interface shows the reviewed loading state

#### Scenario: No truck is found

- **WHEN** the backend returns the reviewed no-match response
- **THEN** the interface shows the reviewed empty state

#### Scenario: Search fails

- **WHEN** the request returns a reviewed error response
- **THEN** the interface shows the corresponding error state
Apply two checks to this delta. First, confirm that it would still make sense if the generated TypeScript method received a different name. Second, replace broad wording such as “corresponding error state” with the accepted message or state when the decision record provides one.

text:
8.7 Turn the handoff into ordered tasks
Use the full-stack task lists to expose waiting points instead of implying that both agents can work independently from the first minute. Keep repository-local work in its own tasks.md, then repeat the contract handoff in both lists.
The backend sequence might include:
## 1. API behavior

- [ ] 1.1 Implement the reviewed input and search behavior.
- [ ] 1.2 Map match, no-match, and invalid-input outcomes to the reviewed responses.
- [ ] 1.3 Add focused tests for every backend scenario.

## 2. Contract handoff

- [ ] 2.1 Generate the OpenAPI document from the implemented API.
- [ ] 2.2 Compare its constraints, schemas, and responses with the delta specification.
- [ ] 2.3 Publish the reviewed document for the frontend change.
The frontend sequence might include:
## 1. Contract intake

- [ ] 1.1 Obtain the reviewed OpenAPI document from `add-unit-number-search-api`.
- [ ] 1.2 Generate the TypeScript client without hand-editing generated files.

## 2. Search interaction

- [ ] 2.1 Implement the reviewed input and submission behavior.
- [ ] 2.2 Render loading, result, empty, and error states from the generated client response.
- [ ] 2.3 Add focused tests for every frontend scenario.
- [ ] 2.4 Run the cross-application unit-number search path.
Block client generation until the backend publishes a reviewed contract. For every task, name the expected test, generated artifact, or review evidence so that a changed file alone cannot satisfy the checkbox.

8.8 Inspect the generated changes with OpenSpec
Use Copilot Chat to draft and revise the artifacts, then use the terminal to inspect OpenSpec’s view of each change:
openspec status --change add-unit-number-search-api
openspec validate add-unit-number-search-api

text:
8.9 Review both changes as one capability
Open the backend and frontend changes side by side. Follow behavior from the user’s action to the API response and back to the rendered state:









Review path
Backend evidence
Frontend evidence
Question




Valid submission
Request constraint and success scenario
Input and submission scenario
Do both use the same accepted input rule?


Match
Response scenario and schema decision
Result-state scenario
Can the generated contract supply every displayed field?


No match
Reviewed API response
Empty-state scenario
Does the UI interpret the response without redefining it?


Invalid input
Validation response
Immediate feedback and response handling
Could the UI permit input that the API rejects?


Failure
Error contract
Error-state scenario
Which failures receive distinct user-visible treatment?



Look for drift that valid Markdown would not catch:

Does one change say “exact” while the other implies partial matching?
Does the frontend expect one result while the backend returns a collection, or the reverse?
Does either design introduce normalization absent from the behavioral delta?
Does a task add VIN search, pagination, filtering, or another deferred capability?
Does every scenario lead to implementation and verification work?

Ask Copilot for a review rather than another rewrite when the drafts are complete:
Review these two OpenSpec changes as one full-stack capability without editing them.

Trace every accepted decision from the Chapter 7 record through the backend and frontend
proposals, delta specifications, designs, and tasks.  Report contradictions, unsupported
assumptions, duplicated contract definitions, missing scenarios, broken dependency order, and
tasks with no requirement.  Cite the artifact and heading for each finding.
Still give the agent’s report a human review. In particular, verify whether a cited “contradiction” represents a real behavioral mismatch or an intentional difference between an API response and its user-facing presentation.

title: 9  Applying the Spring Boot Change
text:
9.1 Learning objective
What happens when a reviewed OpenSpec plan meets an existing Spring Boot codebase? Use the apply workflow to find out one task at a time. Let Copilot inspect the active change and nearby code, then require a focused test before it checks off the task. If the repository contradicts the plan, pause and repair the artifact that owns the decision.
Use this chapter to apply the backend unit-number change without reducing OpenSpec to a prompt template. title: 9  Applying the Spring Boot Change
text:
9.2 Move from artifacts to code
The proposal workflow answered, “What change should the team review?” Apply asks a different question: “What code and evidence would satisfy the reviewed change in this repository?”
Keep the four planning artifacts in distinct roles while answering it:








Artifact
Question during apply
Reason to pause




proposal.md
Does this edit remain inside the accepted purpose and scope?
The implementation introduces a deferred capability or affects an unnamed system


Delta spec.md
Which observable result must this task produce?
The scenario cannot determine a request, response, or error outcome


design.md
Which technical boundary and trade-off should guide the edit?
The codebase disproves an assumption or requires a consequential new choice


tasks.md
What remains, and what evidence would justify checking it off?
The task has no matching requirement, test, or reviewable output



Do not ask Copilot to implement from tasks.md alone. A task such as “add the search endpoint” cannot settle the accepted matching rule, response shape, or no-match behavior. Require the workflow to read the proposal, delta specification, and design before treating the checklist as executable work.






NoteApply does not approve the plan



Treat a reviewed plan as the current implementation target, not as an infallible prediction. If the code exposes a missing behavior or an impossible design assumption, return to the owning artifact and review the correction before continuing.

9.3 Check readiness before changing code
Start in the backend repository and inspect the active change from the terminal:
openspec status --change add-unit-number-search-api
openspec validate add-unit-number-search-api
openspec show add-unit-number-search-api
Look for the expected change name, complete planning artifacts, structurally valid requirements, and unchecked implementation tasks. Then read the files themselves; structural validation cannot decide whether the team chose the right behavior.
Before invoking apply, answer these questions from the artifacts:

Which unit-number inputs should the API accept or reject?
What should a client observe for a match and for no match?
Which error responses belong to this change?
Which existing controller, service, and persistence boundaries should remain in place?
Which test command and OpenAPI generation path does the repository use?
Which capabilities, such as VIN or partial search, remain outside this change?

If any answer requires a guess, stop there. A more detailed prompt should not substitute for a missing product decision, and an implementation convention should not quietly become new API behavior.
Also check the worktree before delegating edits. Note which files already contain user changes and locate the nearest comparable search path. Ask Copilot to preserve unrelated work and inspect the nearest implementation and test before creating another abstraction.

text:
9.4 Start a bounded apply session
Name the change when more than one active change could be selected:
/opsx:apply add-unit-number-search-api
The installed workflow should read the change context, find pending tasks in tasks.md, implement them, and mark completed checkboxes as work progresses. Strengthen that invocation with a bounded request when repository details or review expectations deserve emphasis:
/opsx:apply add-unit-number-search-api

Apply the next unchecked backend task from the active change.

Before editing:
- read proposal.md, the unit-number-search delta specification, design.md, and tasks.md;
- inspect the existing controller, service, repository, and nearest tests; and
- state which scenario the task should satisfy and which focused check could disprove the edit.

During implementation:
- preserve the existing Spring Boot boundaries described by the design;
- keep VIN, partial search, and frontend behavior outside this change;
- do not invent a response or validation rule when the artifacts are silent; and
- preserve unrelated worktree changes.

After editing, run the narrow test named by the repository or task.  Mark the task complete only
after the code, assertion, and test output agree.  Pause and report contradictions or missing
decisions instead of choosing behavior on the team's behalf.
Start with one unchecked task so that a focused test can reject the implementation before the same mistake spreads through controller, service, repository, contract, and test code. A tightly coupled pair of edits may need to land together; ask Copilot to explain that dependency and run the narrowest useful check afterward.
The editor need not change the source of truth. In VS Code, invoke the installed OPSX prompt from Copilot Chat and attach only the files needed to resolve the current task. In IntelliJ IDEA, use the corresponding installed workflow and working-set controls. In either client, judge the result against the same repository artifacts and commands.

title: 9  Applying the Spring Boot Change
section: 9.5 Follow a scenario through the backend
text:
9.5 Follow a scenario through the backend
Choose one scenario before choosing files. Trace a matching unit number through the application:
delta scenario
    |
    v
request validation -> controller mapping -> service decision -> repository query
    |                                                        |
    +---------------- focused assertions --------------------+
                             |
                             v
                    generated OpenAPI document
Use this path as an inspection guide, not as permission to add every layer. If the repository already keeps validation in a request type or delegates search directly from a controller to a service, follow that local design unless design.md explicitly changes it.

9.5.1 Keep validation at the API boundary
Start with the accepted input rule, then find the Spring boundary that already validates comparable request values. Reuse its annotation, validator, or error-mapping convention when it can express the reviewed behavior without changing it.
Then write or adapt a focused assertion. Could the test distinguish invalid input from a valid unit number that has no match? Could it catch an implementation that trims, folds case, or accepts partial input when the specification does not permit that transformation?
Avoid deriving the rule from a database column or a frontend control. Those details might suggest a useful implementation, but the backend delta should remain the authority for what a client may send and observe.


9.5.2 Preserve controller and error semantics
Next, inspect the controller or route that owns adjacent search behavior. Follow its response- mapping pattern for successful results, no match, and invalid requests only where that pattern agrees with the reviewed scenarios.
Make assertions at the HTTP boundary for status, body shape, and relevant headers. A service test could prove that no entity was returned while still missing a controller that maps the absence to the wrong response. title: 10  Applying the Angular Change
text:
10.7 Follow one scenario through Angular
Choose a scenario before choosing files. For a matching unit number, trace the path from the delta to the rendered result:
frontend delta scenario
     |
     v
input state -> submit event -> hand-written boundary -> generated client
                |
                v
rendered result <- view state <- response mapping <- backend contract
  |
  +---------------- focused assertions ----------------+
Use the trace to locate existing owners, not to require a new layer at every arrow. If the repository already calls generated services through a facade, extend that facade. If the local design keeps a small interaction in the component, avoid introducing a store merely because the diagram contains a state step.

10.7.1 Bind input behavior to the scenario
Implement only client-side rules approved by the frontend delta. Keep immediate feedback useful, but do not present it as final API enforcement. A stale browser, a direct API caller, or a changed contract can bypass the Angular validator, so keep backend validation authoritative.
Test the distinction between these paths:

input that the accepted rule rejects before submission;
valid input that produces no match;
valid input that produces a matching result; and
a request that fails after valid submission.

Ask whether the component prevents an invalid request, displays feedback at the specified time, and clears or retains prior state exactly as the scenario requires. Avoid deriving new rules from an HTML attribute or generated model comment when the delta remains silent.


10.7.2 Make request transitions visible
Model only states that a user or test needs to distinguish. Check the initial, loading, result, empty, and error paths against the actual delta rather than treating this list as a product decision.
For each transition, settle what should happen to prior output. Record whether a second submission clears an old result, whether the UI ignores a stale response after a newer request finishes, and whether an error preserves the entered unit number for correction or retry. Put accepted answers in the frontend delta or design before encoding them in RxJS operators, signals, or component fields.
Use the Angular mechanism already chosen by the repository and reviewed design. Whether the code uses signals, observables, reactive forms, or another established pattern, require the same observable outcomes and test them at the interaction boundary.


10.7.3 Keep transport details behind the generated boundary
Route requests through the generated client and the repository’s hand-written service or facade when one exists. Do not duplicate URL paths, serialize a parallel request body, or cast an unrecognized response until TypeScript stops objecting.
When the generated API feels awkward, inspect the OpenAPI document and generator configuration first. Wrap a transport-shaped method behind a small application boundary when the contract remains correct; return to the backend owner when the contract itself fails to express the reviewed behavior.

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.1 Learning objective
The backend and frontend implementations now exist in separate repositories. Before closing either change, test a stronger claim than “the code passes.” The artifacts must be valid, the code must match the accepted scenarios, the two applications must agree on the contract, and the main specifications must receive the behavior that shipped.
OpenSpec separates that work into distinct checks. Use artifact validation to examine the change’s structure. Use implementation verification to compare code and tests with the accepted artifacts. Review synchronization when archival merges the delta into the main specs. Then inspect the archive as the retained history of the decision. None of these checks substitutes for the others.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to use openspec validate and /opsx:verify for their different purposes, review the main-spec update produced during archival, and preserve the reason and identity of a change after active work ends.

Run these checks in order. Failed artifact validation leaves implementation review without a stable target. A missing implementation scenario makes the proposed main-spec update premature. An unexpected spec diff should stop archival before it records the wrong behavior.
Capture the result in the pull request, issue, or team review record:

Scenario verification: pass, <focused test commands>

11.3 Reestablish the change boundary
Start by recovering the accepted scope from each repository. In this lab, the backend change is add-unit-number-search-api, and the frontend change is add-unit-number-search-ui. A shared Jira issue or cross-repository identifier connects them as one product change without erasing repository ownership.
Run the inspection commands from the root of each repository:
openspec status --change add-unit-number-search-api
openspec show add-unit-number-search-api
openspec validate add-unit-number-search-api --strict
openspec status --change add-unit-number-search-ui
openspec show add-unit-number-search-ui
openspec validate add-unit-number-search-ui --strict
Use status to inspect artifact completion, show to read the change and its deltas, and validate to find structural problems such as a malformed delta or a requirement without a scenario. These commands do not prove that Angular sent the expected request or that Spring Boot returned the accepted response. Implementation verification covers that question.
Read the artifacts after the commands finish. Do not let a successful exit code replace checking that the CLI resolved the intended OpenSpec root, selected the intended change, and examined the files just reviewed. In a repository with several active changes, validating the wrong change provides reassuring but irrelevant output.






NoteValidation checks artifacts, not application behavior

11.4 Verify the implementation against the artifacts
Open each repository in turn, select the named change, and run OpenSpec’s verification skill:
/opsx:verify
Review its findings under completeness, correctness, and coherence. Check that every task is complete, each requirement has corresponding code and tests, and the implementation still follows the reviewed design. The skill reports findings but does not block archival, so decide how to resolve each warning before proceeding.
If the frontend report finds all tasks checked but no focused test for the no-match scenario, keep the change open and add the missing evidence. A user-visible state in the accepted delta deserves a stronger response than an optional naming cleanup.
Use the report to guide inspection, then confirm its claims in the repository. An agent can miss a test hidden behind an unfamiliar convention, infer correspondence from similar names, or accept a checked task without reproducing its command. Connect every accepted scenario to code and to a check that fails when the behavior breaks.

11.4.1 Build a scenario-to-evidence map
Map the unit-number scenarios before running a broad final suite:









Accepted scenario
Backend evidence
Frontend evidence
Cross-repository evidence




Invalid unit number
Request validation test
Submission and feedback test
Browser confirms that invalid input does not produce a search result


Matching unit
Controller or service test for the reviewed response
Component test for the result state
Browser displays data returned by the running backend


No matching unit
API test for the reviewed no-match contract
Component test for the empty state
Browser distinguishes no match from request failure


Request failure
Error-contract test where specified
Component test for the error and retry path
Integrated test or controlled failure evidence where practical



Include only scenarios from the accepted delta specifications. If the change does not define retry behavior, omit that assertion or return to the change for a reviewed decision before implementing it.
Run focused checks before broad suites. Use each repository’s package, build, and test configuration rather than inventing generic commands. Preserve the exact commands and results in the review record:
Backend scenario: matching unit
Command: <repository-configured focused Spring Boot test>
Result: pass

Frontend scenario: no matching unit
Command: <repository-configured focused Angular test>
Result: pass

Integrated scenario: matching unit from browser through API
Command: <repository-configured Playwright test>
Result: pass


11.4.2 Follow the contract across repositories
Review the cross-repository path because each repository can pass in isolation while the product path fails. Start with the backend-owned OpenAPI document and confirm that it generated the Angular client under test. Then trace one accepted example through the browser, generated client, HTTP boundary, backend implementation, and rendered result.
For a matching unit, check these handoffs:

Confirm that the browser submits the input accepted by the frontend delta.
Confirm that the generated client sends the request described by the reviewed OpenAPI operation.
Compare the backend status and response shape with the API document.
Trace the response through the frontend without introducing another contract.
Compare the rendered fields and state with the frontend scenario.

Repeat the path for distinctions that often disappear at a repository boundary, especially no match versus request failure. Backend tests can distinguish their status codes, and component tests can distinguish views built from mocked values. Use the integrated path to show that the generated client carries the distinction between them.
When a mismatch appears, repair the boundary that owns it. A backend response that contradicts the reviewed OpenAPI document belongs in the backend change. A correct generated response that produces the wrong visible state belongs in the frontend implementation or delta. Do not change the main specification merely to match whichever behavior happened to ship.

title: 11  Verifying, Synchronizing, and Archiving
text:
11.6 Understand synchronization during archive
In the current OpenSpec CLI workflow, archiving normally performs the specification update. The command validates the change, previews its effect on openspec/specs/, merges the delta after confirmation, and moves the change directory under openspec/changes/archive/.
Here, synchronization means reviewing that transfer from active delta to main specification. Keep code generation, deployment, and cross-repository contract exchange in their own workflows. Never rewrite a requirement during archival simply to match the implementation.
Before running archive, inspect the relevant main spec and active delta side by side:

identify every requirement to be added, modified, removed, or renamed;
match modified requirements to their identities in the main spec;
check that no condition or scenario disappears during the merge;
remove behavior that was not accepted for this change; and
compare the resulting main-spec behavior with the implementation just verified.

Then run archive interactively so that its proposed spec updates remain visible:
openspec archive add-unit-number-search-api
Review the preview before confirming it. After the command completes, inspect the repository diff:
git diff -- openspec/specs openspec/changes
Repeat the process in the frontend repository with its own change:
openspec archive add-unit-number-search-ui
git diff -- openspec/specs openspec/changes
Expect the diff to show the accepted requirements in the main specs and the dated change directory under the archive. Stop before commit if it contains unrelated specification edits, missing scenarios, or an unexpected capability name.
For agents or CI, --yes can answer archive confirmations non-interactively:
openspec archive add-unit-number-search-api --yes
--yes removes the prompt, not the review obligation. Inspect the proposed update beforehand or review the resulting diff before accepting the commit.
Reserve --skip-specs for changes that do not update main specifications, such as some tooling or documentation changes. Do not use it for the unit-number feature: that would archive the delta while leaving the main source of truth behind. Likewise, do not use --no-validate to bypass a malformed change.

11.9 Run the fresh-session test
After archival, start a Copilot session without the transcript from Chapters 8 through 10. Point it to the repository artifacts:
From the current main specs and archived OpenSpec changes:

1. What unit-number search behavior is currently accepted?
2. Which archived change introduced it, and why?
3. Which scenarios distinguish invalid input, no match, and request failure?
4. Which related change belongs to the other repository?

title: 12  Adding VIN Search to a Brownfield System
text:
12.1 Learning objective
Suppose the unit-number search from the earlier chapters has shipped. The backend endpoint, OpenAPI document, generated Angular client, form validation, and result states now work together. Then a product owner asks for one more way to find a truck: “Could users search by VIN too?”
The request sounds small, but it leaves product decisions hidden inside the word “too.” Will VIN use the current operation or a separate one? How will a user choose the search mode? Which unit-number behaviors must survive unchanged? If a coding agent answers from nearby code, its implementation may turn local precedent into product policy before anyone reviews the choice.
How might OpenSpec keep those decisions visible? Describe the requested difference instead of reconstructing every choice behind the application. The resulting delta can define VIN behavior, while the proposal and verification plan can protect the accepted unit-number path.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to propose an additive VIN-search change in a brownfield system without pretending that the whole system was specified from the beginning. You should also be able to trace that change through OpenSpec artifacts, the backend-owned API contract, the generated Angular client, and regression evidence for the behavior already in use.

text:
12.4 Decide whether VIN search is additive
An ADDED delta would fit when VIN introduces another search path while the accepted unit-number path remains valid. A MODIFIED delta would fit if the request changes the meaning of an existing requirement, such as replacing a unit-number-only input with a single identifier field whose rules now vary by mode.
Do not infer the delta operation from the screen layout. One form could expose two independent capabilities, while two controls could call a single revised API operation. Choose ADDED or MODIFIED from the observable contract and the identity of the accepted requirement.
For this chapter, assume the reviewed direction is additive:

a VIN search accepts a full 17-character VIN;
a user can choose unit-number or VIN mode;
the existing unit-number path keeps its accepted behavior; and
result and error behavior may be shared only where the accepted specifications say so.

Those assumptions should remain visible in the proposal. If the product owner has not decided case normalization, whitespace handling, disallowed VIN characters, no-match behavior, or the fields shown in a result, use open questions rather than letting Copilot infer answers.

- assumptions in code or tests that only permit unit-number search;
- generated files or external contracts that should not be edited by hand; and
- unresolved product decisions that would change observable behavior.

section: 12.6 Coordinate one product change across two repositories
text:
12.6 Coordinate one product change across two repositories
The earlier lab chapters established a separate OpenSpec root in each repository. Continue that model here with one active backend change and one active frontend change. Give the backend change ownership of VIN API behavior and contract publication; give the frontend change ownership of mode selection, input feedback, and rendering.
OpenSpec now also documents beta stores for planning one change across several repositories.1 A team using that model could keep the shared artifacts in a store and expose them to both code repositories. The ownership and contract questions in this chapter would still apply, even though the artifact layout would differ.
Possible change names might be:
commercial-truck-search-api/
`-- openspec/changes/add-vin-search-api/

commercial-truck-search-ui/
`-- openspec/changes/add-vin-search-ui/
A shared work-item identifier could connect the changes. Their proposals should also name the handoff directly: the frontend client generation waits for a reviewed backend OpenAPI document. That dependency may slow parallel work, but it reduces the chance that the repositories invent different VIN contracts.
The backend proposal could define this boundary:
# Change: Add VIN search API

## Why

Users need to locate a truck when a VIN is available instead of a unit number.

## What Changes

- Add API behavior for search by a full 17-character VIN.
- Publish the reviewed VIN request and response behavior in OpenAPI.
- Preserve accepted unit-number search behavior.

## Non-Goals

- Combined VIN and unit-number queries
- Partial VIN search
- Changes to accepted unit-number validation or responses

## Dependencies

- The frontend change may regenerate its client after review of the updated OpenAPI document.
The frontend proposal could remain narrower:
# Change: Add VIN search mode

## Why

Users need to choose VIN when that is the identifier available for a truck.

## What Changes

- Add a control for choosing unit-number or VIN search.
- Apply the reviewed validation rule for the selected mode.
- Send VIN searches through the generated API client.
- Preserve the accepted unit-number interaction.

## Non-Goals

- Handwritten API request or response types
- Simultaneous search by both identifiers
- Changes to accepted result fields unless separately reviewed
Notice what these proposals do not decide. Neither chooses an Angular component structure, Java method name, database index, or generated-client class. Those choices may belong in design.md after the team agrees on behavior.

title: 12  Adding VIN Search to a Brownfield System
section: 12.7 Write deltas that expose the additive boundary
text:
12.7 Write deltas that expose the additive boundary
The backend delta should make VIN behavior testable without copying the complete unit-number specification. With unresolved details still visible, it might begin like this:
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Search by VIN

The API SHALL accept a full 17-character VIN and return the reviewed search outcome.

#### Scenario: VIN has the required length

- **WHEN** a client searches with a VIN containing exactly 17 characters
- **THEN** the API evaluates the VIN according to the reviewed search rules

#### Scenario: VIN has the wrong length

- **WHEN** a client searches with a VIN containing fewer or more than 17 characters
- **THEN** the API returns the reviewed validation response

#### Scenario: No truck matches the VIN

- **WHEN** a client searches with a valid VIN that matches no truck
- **THEN** the API returns [the reviewed no-match response]
Do not add a second copy of the accepted unit-number requirement merely to say that it remains in force. Keep preservation visible in the proposal’s non-goals, implementation tasks, and regression evidence. If VIN work changes the accepted unit-number contract after all, revise the proposal and write a complete MODIFIED requirement for that behavior.
The frontend delta might separate mode selection from mode-specific validation:
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Select a search mode

The interface SHALL let the user choose unit-number or VIN search mode.

#### Scenario: User selects VIN mode

- **WHEN** the user selects VIN mode
- **THEN** the interface applies the reviewed VIN input and validation behavior

#### Scenario: User returns to unit-number mode

- **WHEN** the user selects unit-number mode
- **THEN** the interface applies the accepted unit-number behavior

### Requirement: Validate a VIN search

The interface SHALL accept a full 17-character VIN for submission.

#### Scenario: VIN is not 17 characters

- **WHEN** the user attempts to submit a VIN with fewer or more than 17 characters
- **THEN** the interface prevents submission and shows the reviewed validation feedback
Would switching modes clear the input, retain it, or revalidate it? Would the visible label and accessible name change with the selected mode? Would a VIN result show the same fields as a unit-number result? Each answer could affect a user-visible scenario, so unanswered cases should remain open rather than falling into component code by accident.

text:
12.8 Design the contract handoff
The backend should continue to own the wire contract. After implementing the reviewed VIN API behavior, generate or update the OpenAPI document and compare it with the delta before publishing it to the frontend repository.
At minimum, inspect:

how the operation distinguishes VIN from unit-number search;
whether the VIN constraint appears in the request schema;
which success, no-match, validation, and failure responses are documented; and
whether existing unit-number schemas or operations changed unexpectedly.

Only then should the frontend regenerate its TypeScript client. Editing generated code by hand might make a local build pass, but the next generation would erase the fix and conceal disagreement with the backend contract.
This sequence need not block all frontend work. The team could implement the mode control and local validation against the reviewed frontend delta while waiting for the contract. Integration through the generated client, however, should wait until the backend-owned document has passed review.

12.9 Apply the change in dependency order
A task list can make that partial parallelism visible:

Add backend scenarios for valid VIN, invalid length, match, and the reviewed no-match behavior.
Implement the VIN path without changing accepted unit-number behavior.
Generate and inspect the OpenAPI document, including a diff of existing operations.
Add the frontend mode control and mode-specific validation.

Connect VIN submission and result handling through the generated client.
Run focused backend, frontend, and browser checks for VIN and unit-number paths.

At each step, compare the implementation with the relevant requirement. Treat a checked task as a work record, not proof that the resulting behavior matches the delta.
Copilot may suggest consolidating both search modes behind one helper or component state model. Before accepting the refactor, check whether the abstraction preserves each mode’s validation and error rules. Two explicit paths may be easier to verify when the only gain would be less repeated code.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.1 Learning objective
The unit-number search from the earlier chapters has already passed review, reached both repositories, and entered the accepted OpenSpec specification. Now suppose a product owner asks for a smaller limit: “Could unit numbers have a maximum of 10 characters instead of requiring 15?”
That request may look like a one-line validation edit. Adding a second requirement, however, would leave two current rules for the same input: one requiring 15 characters and another allowing no more than 10. Developers, reviewers, and later Copilot sessions would have to guess which one wins.
OpenSpec treats this situation as a modification. The change would identify the accepted requirement, provide its complete replacement, and preserve every scenario that should remain part of that requirement. After archive, the main specification should describe one current rule, without asking readers to reconstruct precedence from change dates.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to decide when a request modifies accepted behavior rather than adding a separate capability. You should also be able to write a complete MODIFIED requirement, trace its consequences through two repositories, and verify that archive would leave one coherent source of truth.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.2 Recognize a replacement
Chapter 12 added VIN search without changing the identity of unit-number search. VIN introduced a new way to find a truck, so its requirement could sit beside the accepted unit-number requirement. The request in this chapter behaves differently. A unit number cannot remain both exactly 15 characters and at most 10 characters under the same conditions.
Before choosing a delta operation, complete this sentence:

After this change, the accepted requirement named Search by unit number should …

If the answer begins “still apply, plus users can do something separate,” ADDED may fit. If the answer begins “mean something different,” MODIFIED deserves closer attention. Removing the behavior entirely may call for REMOVED, while changing only its identity may call for RENAMED.







Question
Likely operation




Will a separate requirement coexist with the accepted one?
ADDED


Will the accepted requirement keep its identity but change meaning?
MODIFIED


Will the accepted requirement cease to apply?
REMOVED


Will its identity change while its intended behavior remains?
RENAMED



Implementation files cannot settle this choice on their own. Two validators might share a helper even though they implement separate requirements, while one requirement might span an API, generated client, form, and several tests. The operation follows the relationship between accepted and proposed behavior, not the number or shape of files involved.






WarningA newer sentence does not cancel an older requirement



Appending “Unit numbers SHALL contain no more than 10 characters” under ADDED Requirements would leave the accepted 15-character rule in force. Neither recency nor proximity supplies replacement semantics. Use MODIFIED when review intends one requirement to supersede its accepted version.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.3 Recover the accepted baseline
Before drafting a replacement, inspect the requirement as it exists under openspec/specs/. Record its heading exactly, along with every scenario nested beneath it. OpenSpec uses that requirement identity when applying the delta, and those scenarios reveal behavior that a short change request might otherwise erase.
For the lab, the baseline investigation might ask:

Does the requirement say exactly 15 characters, or no more than 15?
Does it describe trimming or another form of normalization?
Which cases cover matching, no match, empty input, and invalid input?
Do the backend and frontend specifications express the same boundary?
Which tests provide evidence for each accepted scenario?

A small baseline table can keep evidence separate from decisions:









Topic
Accepted source
Implementation evidence
Decision needed?




Length rule
Main unit-number specification
Backend and frontend boundary tests
Yes, replace 15 with the reviewed rule


Normalization
Accepted scenarios, if present
Controller, form, and tests
Only if the request leaves it unclear


Empty input
Accepted scenarios, if present
Validation tests
Only if the new meaning could differ


Match and no match
Accepted scenarios
Service, component, and browser tests
Usually preserve unless scope says otherwise



If the specification, code, and tests disagree, record the mismatch as a review finding. Do not choose whichever behavior is easiest to edit. The team may resolve the mismatch inside this change when it affects the revised rule, or record separate work when it does not. Either choice should remain visible in the proposal.

13.4 Separate the request from its unanswered questions
“Maximum of 10 characters” answers less than it first appears to. Before proposal, the team still needs to decide:

whether values shorter than 10 characters qualify;
whether normalization occurs before the length check;
how the system handles empty and oversized values; and
whether case handling, matching, and no-match behavior change with the boundary.

An exploration prompt could make those gaps visible before proposal begins:
/opsx:explore

We are considering changing the accepted unit-number rule from 15 characters to a maximum of 10.

Please identify:
- the accepted requirement and all of its scenarios;
- every backend and frontend boundary that represents the current length rule;
- generated files and contracts affected by the rule;
- behaviors the request does not settle, including normalization and empty input; and
- tests that provide evidence for behavior likely to remain unchanged.

Do not modify files or infer product decisions from the current implementation.
Organize the resulting notes by what changes, what remains, and what still needs a decision:








Category
Example
Treatment in the change




Requested difference
Replace the 15-character rule with a maximum of 10
State in the proposal and delta


Preserved behavior
A valid value with no match keeps the accepted no-match outcome
Restate its scenario in the replacement requirement


Open decision
Whether trimming occurs before the length check
Resolve before apply or mark as blocking



This separation adds a review step before coding. It also exposes disagreements before the backend and Angular repositories implement different interpretations.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
section: 13.5 Write the proposal around the behavioral change
text:
13.5 Write the proposal around the behavioral change
Once review settles the open questions, the proposal can state both the intended difference and the preservation boundary. For this worked example, suppose the team chooses these exercise assumptions:

leading and trailing spaces are removed before validation;
one through 10 remaining characters are valid;
an empty value remains invalid;
11 or more remaining characters are invalid;
matching remains exact; and
a valid value with no match returns no matching trucks.

Those are example product decisions, not consequences of the word MODIFIED. Another team might choose different answers and still use the same OpenSpec operation.
A compact proposal could read:
# Change: Reduce the unit-number length limit

## Why

The business now assigns unit numbers containing between one and 10 characters.  The search still
requires exact matching after removing leading and trailing spaces.

## What Changes

- Remove leading and trailing spaces before validating the unit number.
- Accept between one and 10 remaining characters.
- Reject empty values and values longer than 10 characters.
- Preserve exact matching and the existing no-match result.
- Publish the revised constraint through the backend-owned OpenAPI contract.

## Non-Goals

- Changes to VIN search
- Partial or fuzzy unit-number matching
- New result fields or response states
Naming unchanged behavior limits the change. A length edit can invite nearby cleanup or a new matching strategy, but the non-goals and preservation claims give reviewers a boundary for those edits without copying unrelated specifications into the delta.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.6 Replace the complete requirement
A MODIFIED section should contain the whole requirement as it ought to read after archive. It should not contain a patch fragment such as “change 15 to 10,” because that fragment would depend on a reader finding and mentally merging the accepted version.
Using the exercise assumptions, a backend delta might look like this:
## MODIFIED Requirements

### Requirement: Search by unit number

The API SHALL remove leading and trailing spaces from a unit-number search value.  The remaining
value SHALL contain between one and 10 characters, and the API SHALL match it exactly against unit
numbers.

#### Scenario: Matching unit number is at the maximum length

- **GIVEN** a truck has unit number `TRUCK-1234`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRUCK-1234`
- **THEN** the API returns that truck

#### Scenario: Matching unit number is shorter than the maximum

- **GIVEN** a truck has unit number `TRK-123`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRK-123`
- **THEN** the API returns that truck

#### Scenario: Matching unit number has surrounding spaces

- **GIVEN** a truck has unit number `TRUCK-1234`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `  TRUCK-1234  `
- **THEN** the API returns that truck

#### Scenario: Unit number exceeds the maximum

- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRUCK-12345`
- **THEN** the API rejects the search value as invalid

#### Scenario: Unit number is empty

- **WHEN** a client searches with a value that is empty after removing surrounding spaces
- **THEN** the API rejects the search value as invalid

#### Scenario: No truck matches

- **GIVEN** no truck has unit number `TRUCK-9999`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRUCK-9999`
- **THEN** the API returns no matching trucks
This example is complete only under the stated exercise assumptions. Compare it with the actual lab requirement before using it. If that requirement contains another match, failure, or response scenario, carry the scenario forward unless the proposal deliberately changes or removes it.
The requirement heading deserves special care. If the accepted heading reads Search by unit number, changing it casually to Validate a unit number may prevent a clean identity match or misrepresent the requirement’s scope. Copy the accepted heading, then revise the body and scenarios beneath it.






NoteComplete does not mean duplicated



Completeness applies to the requirement being replaced. The delta need not copy every requirement in the capability, nor should it repeat unrelated VIN behavior. Include the revised requirement and all scenarios that should survive within that requirement.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
text:
13.7 Inspect the delta before implementation
OpenSpec validation can catch malformed delta structure, while a behavioral diff can expose an accidental deletion or an unchanged 15-character clause. Run the repository’s configured checks, then inspect the proposed difference:
openspec validate reduce-unit-number-limit --strict
openspec show reduce-unit-number-limit --diff
Review the diff against these checks:

Match the modified heading to the accepted requirement.
Confirm that archive would replace the 15-character wording rather than retain it beside the new rule.
Account for every scenario named by the proposal.
Remove implementation choices, such as Java annotations or Angular validators, from the behavioral specification.
Confirm that each boundary scenario could fail for the intended reason before implementation.

A passing structural check cannot answer all of those questions. Human review still needs to judge whether the replacement captures the business decision and whether its preservation claims are credible.

13.8 Trace one rule through two repositories
The modified requirement may be small, but the old constraint may have crossed several ownership boundaries. Search for the old value and for the concepts that express it. A literal search for 15 could find noise and miss a named constant, a schema facet, or prose that says “fifteen,” so combine value searches with searches for requirement names, validation messages, and test cases.








Boundary

Automated tests

The backend should continue to own the wire contract. After its validation and OpenAPI output reflect the reviewed delta, inspect the contract diff before regenerating the Angular client. Form tests and UI changes may proceed against the reviewed frontend delta, but client integration should wait for the backend-owned contract if generation is the established handoff.
Avoid editing generated client files as though they owned the rule. A manual fix could make the current branch compile, yet regeneration would restore whatever the OpenAPI document still says. The durable correction belongs in the source contract and generation workflow.

title: 13  Modifying Accepted Behavior
section: 13.9 Apply in an order that preserves evidence
text:
13.9 Apply in an order that preserves evidence
A task list might keep the dependency visible without prescribing every class or function:

Add or revise backend tests for 10-character, shorter valid, 11-character, and empty values.
Update backend validation while preserving accepted match, no-match, and error behavior.
Generate and review the OpenAPI document for the revised constraint and unrelated drift.
Regenerate the Angular client from the reviewed contract.
Update Angular validation, visible feedback, and focused component tests.
Exercise the integrated path and rerun preserved-behavior tests in both repositories.

Begin with boundary evidence. A test for exactly 10 characters and another for 11 can show whether the implementation changed the intended edge rather than merely replacing one constant. Tests for matching and no match then check the proposal’s claim that the rest of the search behavior survived.
During apply, ask Copilot to work from scenario names and report the evidence for each one. A message such as “updated max length everywhere” would reveal little about normalization, generated artifacts, or regression coverage. A scenario-to-test trace gives the reviewer something more specific to inspect.

text:
13.10 Verify the replacement before archive
Verification has two jobs: show that the implementation adopted the new boundary and show that the change preserved everything it claimed not to alter.







Claim
Focused evidence




A normalized 10-character value is accepted
Backend boundary test and Angular form test


A normalized value shorter than 10 is accepted
Backend and frontend validation tests


An 11-character value is rejected
API validation test and visible-feedback test


Empty input follows the reviewed rule
Backend and Angular empty-input tests


Match and no-match behavior remain intact
Existing service, component, and integrated tests


Both repositories share the revised contract
Reviewed OpenAPI diff and generated-client diff


The old rule no longer survives
Search across specs, code, generated output, tests, and UI text



Run focused checks first, then the broader repository suites and integrated path. If an 11-character value fails in the UI but reaches the backend through another path, the replacement has not reached every boundary. If all tests pass while the generated schema still reports 15, the repositories still disagree about their contract.
Before archive, inspect the source-of-truth result that synchronization would produce. Confirm that the main specification would contain one complete unit-number requirement with the 10-character maximum and every preserved scenario. If understanding the current rule still requires an older archived change, the active delta remains incomplete.
After archive, repeat the obsolete-assumption search against the main specification and generated artifacts. The dated change record may retain the old rule as history; the active source of truth should not present it as current behavior.

13.12 Verification checkpoint
The change may be ready to close when the modified heading matches the accepted requirement, the delta supplies its complete replacement, and strict validation passes. Focused tests should cover both sides of the new boundary, while regression evidence should cover the scenarios promised as unchanged. The OpenAPI and generated-client diffs should describe the same maximum, and a search should find no current 15-character assumption outside historical records.
If one of those checks fails, keep the change open. Update the artifact that owns the discrepancy, repeat the narrow check, and inspect the would-be source of truth again before archive.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.1 Learning objective
Implementation has started on a Fleet Origin State filter. The backend already handles part of the request when the product owner asks for another filter: Active Status, with values of Active and Decommissioned.
Continuing from that conversation would leave the code ahead of the active proposal. Opening a second change could split one result-filtering rule across two plans. Discarding the first change would lose work that may still fit. Instead, pause implementation and revise the active OpenSpec change until its proposal, delta specifications, design, and tasks describe the new outcome.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to revise an active OpenSpec change without confusing proposed behavior with accepted behavior. You should also be able to decide whether to revise or split the change, reassess partial implementation, and determine when /opsx:apply can resume.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
section: 14.2 Treat the active change as the current plan
text:
14.2 Treat the active change as the current plan
An OpenSpec change under openspec/changes/<change-name>/ describes behavior that has not yet joined the accepted specifications. Some tasks may already be checked, but archive has not made the delta part of openspec/specs/.
That distinction matters when the request changes:








State
Where current behavior lives
How a new decision would usually enter




Accepted behavior
openspec/specs/
A new change with an ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED, or RENAMED delta


Proposed behavior
openspec/changes/<change-name>/
A revision to that active change, when the scope still belongs together


Implemented but unarchived behavior
Code and tests, plus the active change
A revision to the artifacts followed by reassessment of the implementation



Suppose the active delta contains an ADDED requirement named Filter vehicles by fleet origin state. Adding Active Status does not turn that block into a MODIFIED requirement. The team is editing a proposed addition, not replacing an accepted requirement. Chapter 13 used MODIFIED because the target requirement already lived under openspec/specs/.






WarningDo not archive the old plan to make revision easier



Do not archive the old plan merely to create a new baseline. That would move unverified behavior toward the accepted specifications. Keep the change active while its scope and evidence remain unsettled.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.3 Recover the interruption point
Before editing, recover the state of the named change:
For a change named add-vehicle-filters, start with:
openspec status --change add-vehicle-filters
openspec show add-vehicle-filters --diff
openspec validate add-vehicle-filters --strict
Use status to find the available artifacts and checked tasks. Use show --diff to inspect the proposal and requirement deltas. Use validate to find structural problems. A clean validation result cannot show whether the artifacts agree with the revised request.
Read the files as a set after running those commands. For each artifact, ask a different question:







Artifact
Question after the interruption




proposal.md
Does the reason and scope still describe the outcome the product owner wants?


specs/**/spec.md
Could every requirement and scenario still be accepted as written?


design.md
Can the chosen API, query, and UI design represent the revised behavior?


tasks.md
Which checked tasks still produce evidence for the revised scenarios?



Inspect the implementation in the same pass without treating it as the source of the new business rule. Existing query logic may reveal that AND is easy to implement or that an empty parameter already has a meaning. Record the product decision in the change instead of inheriting whichever behavior the code happens to contain.
