title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
text:
14.4 Name the decision that moved
“Add Active Status” sounds specific until it meets the existing filter. Several decisions may still be open:

Should Active Status narrow the same result set as Fleet Origin State?
Should selecting both filters use AND or OR?
Should one control be optional, or must the user choose both values?
Should no selection omit a query parameter, send an empty value, or mean “all”?
Should the result list distinguish no matches from a failed request?
Should Active Status use a fixed set of values or accept arbitrary text?

Record answers before asking an agent to continue implementation. For this exercise, use the following reviewed decisions:







Topic
Revised decision




Available filters
Fleet Origin State and Active Status


Status values
Active and Decommissioned


Combination rule
When both filters have values, a vehicle must match both


One empty selection
Apply only the populated filter


Both selections empty
Return the unfiltered result set


No matching vehicles
Show the existing empty-results state


Request failure
Preserve the existing error state



These choices belong to the worked example, not to OpenSpec. Another product could require at least one filter or treat an empty selection as invalid. What matters here is that implementation resumes from a reviewed meaning.
An exploration prompt can help expose omissions without changing either artifacts or code:
/opsx:explore add-vehicle-filters

The active change currently adds Fleet Origin State filtering.  The product owner now wants an
optional Active Status filter with values Active and Decommissioned.

Compare the proposal, delta specifications, design, tasks, implementation, and tests.  Identify:
- assumptions that describe only the original one-filter behavior;
- unresolved combination and empty-selection rules;
- completed work that may still satisfy the revised behavior; and
- generated or cross-repository surfaces that may become stale.

Do not edit artifacts or code.  Do not infer product decisions from the implementation.
Explore mode can expose the questions, but its conversation does not revise the source of truth. Move the reviewed answers into the active artifacts.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
section: 14.5 Decide whether to revise or split the change
text:
14.5 Decide whether to revise or split the change
Judge scope from the business outcome rather than the files touched:







Revise the active change when…
Start a separate change when…




The new decision completes or corrects proposed behavior
The new request has value on its own


Reviewers would evaluate both parts as one outcome
Either part could be released or withdrawn independently


One set of scenarios must describe how the behaviors interact
Combining them would hide different risks or owners


The original behavior no longer satisfies the request
The active change still meets its reviewed purpose



Shared files alone should not force a merge. Two independent changes may both touch a search component, while one coherent filter behavior may span a controller, generated client, Angular form, and test suites in two repositories.
For the exercise, keep Active Status in add-vehicle-filters. The two controls define one result set, and neither filter can explain the combination or empty-selection rules alone. Preserve that reasoning in the proposal:
## Revision note

Active Status was added while implementation was in progress.  It remains in this change because
the status and fleet-origin controls jointly determine one vehicle-search result set.  The revised
requirements replace the earlier one-filter proposal rather than adding an independent release.
Keep the note short. A reviewer needs the scope decision, not a diary of the conversation.

title: 14  Revising an In-Flight Change
section: 14.6 Revise the artifacts as a set
text:
14.6 Revise the artifacts as a set
Use OpenSpec’s update skill to revise existing planning artifacts without changing application code:
/opsx:update add-vehicle-filters

Revise this active change to add an optional Active Status filter with values Active and
Decommissioned.  When both filters have values, results must match both.  When one filter is empty,
apply only the populated filter.  When both are empty, return the unfiltered result set.  Preserve
the existing empty-results and request-error states.

Show each proposed artifact revision before writing it.  Do not modify application code.
Review each artifact revision before accepting it. A proposal may have the right scope while its delta omits the both-empty scenario. A correct delta may still conflict with a design that sends empty strings for both parameters.

14.6.1 Revise the proposal boundary
Revise the proposal’s outcome and boundaries. Its What Changes section might move from this:
## What Changes

- Add a Fleet Origin State control to vehicle search.
- Send the selected state to the search API.
- Show vehicles from the selected fleet origin state.
to this:
## What Changes

- Add Fleet Origin State and Active Status controls to vehicle search.
- Support Active and Decommissioned status values.
- Apply both populated filters with AND semantics.
- Omit an unselected filter from the request and preserve the unfiltered result when neither is
    selected.
- Preserve the existing empty-results and request-error states.

## Non-Goals

- Multi-select values within either filter
- Changes to vehicle status definitions
- New sorting or pagination behavior
Replace the stale one-filter wording. Do not leave reviewers to decide whether the first or last version wins.


14.6.2 Rewrite the proposed requirement completely
Suppose the original delta adds a requirement for Fleet Origin State filtering. Revise that proposed requirement into a complete statement of the combined behavior:
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Filter vehicle search results

The search UI SHALL allow a user to filter vehicles by Fleet Origin State and Active Status.  The
available Active Status values SHALL be `Active` and `Decommissioned`.  When both filters have
values, a returned vehicle SHALL match both values.

#### Scenario: Both filters are selected

- **GIVEN** Fleet Origin State is `OH`
- **AND** Active Status is `Active`
- **WHEN** the user applies the filters
- **THEN** every returned vehicle has Fleet Origin State `OH`
- **AND** every returned vehicle has Active Status `Active`

#### Scenario: Only Fleet Origin State is selected

- **GIVEN** Fleet Origin State is `OH`
- **AND** Active Status has no selection
- **WHEN** the user applies the filters
- **THEN** every returned vehicle has Fleet Origin State `OH`

#### Scenario: Only Active Status is selected

- **GIVEN** Fleet Origin State has no selection
- **AND** Active Status is `Decommissioned`
- **WHEN** the user applies the filters
- **THEN** every returned vehicle has Active Status `Decommissioned`

#### Scenario: Neither filter is selected

- **GIVEN** neither filter has a selection
- **WHEN** the user applies the filters
- **THEN** the search returns the unfiltered result set

#### Scenario: No vehicle matches the selected filters

- **GIVEN** no vehicle matches the selected filter values
- **WHEN** the user applies the filters
- **THEN** the UI shows the existing empty-results state
Why keep ADDED here? The filter requirement has not entered the accepted specification, so the team is revising the proposed addition itself. Replacing ADDED with MODIFIED merely because the draft changed would confuse artifact history with delta semantics.
Carry forward any earlier scenarios for resetting filters, preserving pagination, or handling a request failure unless the revision deliberately removes them.


14.6.3 Revisit design decisions
Requirements should describe observable behavior, while the design can explain how the two repositories will represent it. A revised design might include decisions such as:

the backend accepts optional fleetOriginState and activeStatus query parameters;
the query layer adds a predicate only for a populated parameter;
two predicates combine with AND;
the backend-owned OpenAPI document defines the status enum;
the Angular client is regenerated from that document; and
the UI leaves an unselected control absent from the request rather than sending an empty string.

Keep framework details in the design rather than repeating them in every scenario. Also record ownership: if Angular invents its own status union before the backend contract changes, both repositories can compile while disagreeing on capitalization or allowed values.
An impact table can make stale assumptions easier to find:








Surface
Original assumption
Revision to review




API parameters
One optional state value
Two optional values with defined omission behavior


Query construction
One state predicate
Zero, one, or two predicates; two combine with AND


OpenAPI document
State parameter only
Status enum and optional status parameter


Generated client
One filter argument
Regenerated method or request type for both filters


Angular form
One select control
Two controls with independent empty selections


Result states
State-filtered results
Combined results plus preserved empty and error states





14.6.4 Reassess every task checkbox
A checked task records work against the earlier plan. Keep it checked only when its output still supports the revised artifacts.
The task list might change from:
- [x] 1.1 Add the fleet-origin query parameter to the API contract
- [x] 1.2 Implement the fleet-origin query predicate
- [ ] 2.1 Regenerate the Angular client
- [ ] 2.2 Add the Fleet Origin State control
- [ ] 3.1 Add integrated filter tests
to:
- [ ] 1.1 Revise the API contract for optional fleet-origin and active-status parameters
- [ ] 1.2 Implement zero, one, and two-predicate query behavior
- [ ] 1.3 Add backend tests for each filter combination
- [ ] 2.1 Regenerate the Angular client from the revised contract
- [ ] 2.2 Add Fleet Origin State and Active Status controls
- [ ] 2.3 Preserve empty-results and request-error states
- [ ] 3.1 Add integrated tests for empty, single-filter, and combined-filter requests
Reopen both backend tasks if the checked contract and query cannot represent Active Status. Keep a completed request-object task checked if its implementation still satisfies the revised design. Judge the evidence, not the effort already spent.






NoteUpdate changes artifacts, not application code



/opsx:update should revise the existing plan and stop. Resume /opsx:apply only after reviewers accept the updated proposal, requirements, design, and tasks. Keeping those steps separate makes it easier to see whether a code edit came from the reviewed revision or from an agent’s inference.

After editing the artifacts, rerun the three opening checks:
openspec status --change add-vehicle-filters
openspec show add-vehicle-filters --diff
openspec validate add-vehicle-filters --strict
Ask the update skill for a coherence review without supplying another revision:

14.8 Reconcile partial implementation with the revision
Once the revised artifacts pass review, classify the existing work before writing more code:








Finding
Example
Likely treatment




Reusable
The request model already supports optional filter fields
Keep it and retain supporting tests

The API accepts fleet origin but not active status
Extend it under the revised task

Do not discard all partial work or treat every completed line as settled. Code may survive unchanged while its test needs another case because it proves only one branch of the revised rule.

/opsx:apply add-vehicle-filters
Let the apply workflow read the revised artifacts and work through the pending tasks. Mark a task complete only after its implementation and focused checks pass. If coding exposes another unanswered business question, pause apply and return to the artifact that owns the decision.
Suppose the generated client represents an unselected status as undefined, while the backend distinguishes a missing parameter from an empty string. Treat that mismatch as a contract question. Resolve the intended request behavior, revise the delta or design, and then continue the client work.

Test the revised scenarios alongside the behavior the change intends to preserve. A one-filter test suite would provide weak evidence after both filters become part of the request.

Browser distinguishes no match from failure



Run /opsx:verify after the focused repository tests:
/opsx:verify add-vehicle-filters
Use its completeness, correctness, and coherence findings to locate missing evidence or drift. Inspect the cited code and reproduce the relevant commands before deciding that the change is ready to archive.
Search for remnants of the original plan as a final check. Useful terms may include the old requirement heading, the original API parameter, UI labels that mention only Fleet Origin State, handwritten client types, and tests whose names still imply one-filter behavior.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.1 Learning objective
Consider two developers working from the same accepted truck-search specification. One opens add-license-plate-search; the other opens revise-vin-search. Each change has its own proposal, delta specifications, design, tasks, branch, and worktree. Assume that both pass their focused tests.
Reviewed alone, either change could look complete. Read together, they might assign different meanings to the same request, generated client method, or Angular control. The License Plate change could replace a single VIN field with a search-mode control, while the VIN change could revise the accepted VIN length rule around the original field. Git would not have to report a conflict for those designs to be incompatible.
OpenSpec lets each proposal develop without immediately rewriting the accepted specification. That isolation supports parallel work; compatibility still requires a comparison of the proposed behavior. The team would need to settle shared decisions and recheck any proposal that outlives the baseline from which it began.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to coordinate concurrent OpenSpec changes without treating separate folders, branches, or worktrees as evidence of compatibility. You should also be able to find semantic overlap, record a resolution in the active artifacts, and choose a synchronization or archive order that could preserve both business goals.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.2 Separate isolation from coordination
Three mechanisms may appear in a parallel workflow, but each answers a different question:








Mechanism
Question it can answer
Question it cannot answer




OpenSpec change folder
What behavior does this proposal intend to add, modify, or remove?
Would another active proposal make the behavior contradictory?


Git branch
Which commits belong to this line of work?
Do two branches express compatible product decisions?


Git worktree
Can each branch have its own working directory?
Which shared contract should become accepted behavior?



Suppose the branches edit different files. License Plate search could add a controller method, while the VIN change could revise a shared request type. Git might merge both edits cleanly even though the controller sends a request the revised type can no longer represent. Suppose instead that both branches edit the same OpenAPI file. Git might report a textual conflict, but resolving the lines would not decide whether one endpoint should accept mutually exclusive parameters or separate operations.
Begin the coordination review above the file level: Can both sets of requirements be true in one accepted system?






WarningA clean merge is weak evidence



A clean Git merge could show only that the edited lines did not collide. Passing tests on each branch could show only that each implementation satisfies the assumptions available on that branch. Neither result would compare the two proposed meanings.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.3 Establish one comparison point
Parallel changes become harder to reason about when each participant uses a different baseline. Before comparing proposals, name the accepted commit and main specifications from which both changes will be reviewed. That snapshot need not freeze the repository, but it would give reviewers one answer to “accepted before these changes.”
For the exercise, use these two active changes:








Change
Business goal
Intended delta




add-license-plate-search
Let a user find a truck by license plate and jurisdiction
Add another search mode while preserving unit-number and VIN search


revise-vin-search
Change the accepted VIN input rule
Modify VIN validation and request behavior without changing other modes



The business goals could coexist. Their designs might not. Both changes may touch the search-mode selector, shared request shape, OpenAPI operation, generated Angular client, validation messages, and regression suite. Different goals do not provide enough evidence to treat the changes as independent.
Start by checking that both artifacts are structurally readable:
openspec status --change add-license-plate-search
openspec show add-license-plate-search --diff
openspec validate add-license-plate-search --strict

openspec status --change revise-vin-search
openspec show revise-vin-search --diff
openspec validate revise-vin-search --strict
Strict validation could reject malformed deltas. It would not decide whether the two valid deltas contradict each other, so the next review should compare meaning rather than repeat validation.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
section: 15.4 Read each delta in two directions
text:
15.4 Read each delta in two directions
Avoid reading either proposal as a self-contained story. Read it first against the accepted specification and then sideways against every other active change that touches the same capability.
The baseline comparison could ask:

Which accepted requirement does this change assume?
Which behavior would it add, modify, remove, or rename?
Which existing scenarios must remain true?
Which contract, generated artifact, UI state, or test carries that behavior?

The sideways comparison could then ask:

Do both changes alter the same requirement or observable outcome?
Does one proposal depend on a request or response shape that the other would revise?
Do the proposals give different meanings to the same empty, invalid, or no-match state?
Would a scenario from one change fail after the other became the baseline?

A compact worksheet may keep this review grounded:










Surface
Accepted baseline
License Plate delta
VIN delta
Decision needed?




Search mode
Unit Number or VIN
Add License Plate
Preserve existing modes
Could the mode model represent all three?


Request contract
One identifier plus a mode
Add plate and jurisdiction inputs
Revise VIN input constraints
Could invalid parameter combinations be expressed?


Generated client
Current search request
Regenerate for plate fields
Regenerate for VIN rule
Which contract version should generate the client?


Validation
Rules vary by current mode
Add plate and jurisdiction rules
Replace VIN rule
Could validation switch by mode without leaking rules?


Regression behavior
Unit Number and VIN pass
Preserve both modes
Preserve Unit Number
Which VIN scenarios would be replaced rather than preserved?



The coordination work would sit in the last column. “Both touch SearchComponent” would describe file overlap. “License Plate assumes fixed-length VIN while the VIN delta replaces that rule” would identify a behavioral decision that reviewers could settle.

15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
section: 15.5 Ask Copilot to report overlap, not resolve it
text:
15.5 Ask Copilot to report overlap, not resolve it
An exploration pass could help assemble the comparison without granting an agent authority to pick the winning behavior. A prompt such as this would keep the task bounded:
/opsx:explore

Compare the active changes `add-license-plate-search` and `revise-vin-search` with the same accepted
truck-search specifications.

For each change, report:
- requirements and scenarios added, modified, removed, or assumed unchanged;
- shared API, generated-client, UI, validation, and test surfaces;
- assumptions that would become stale if the other change were accepted first; and
- product or contract decisions that the artifacts do not resolve.

Do not edit artifacts or application code.  Do not choose a winner from implementation order.  Distinguish
textual overlap from behavioral overlap.
The resulting report should point to the exact requirements and scenarios in disagreement. If it only lists files, the prompt has not yet reached the decision boundary. A follow-up could ask what observable behavior would differ after both deltas were applied.

15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
section: 15.6 Recognize the forms of semantic overlap
text:
15.6 Recognize the forms of semantic overlap
Some conflicts would announce themselves through the same requirement name. Others might hide behind different language or different repositories. The following patterns deserve a closer comparison:

Both deltas modify the identity or meaning of one accepted requirement.
One delta adds behavior under a condition that the other delta removes.
Two deltas assign different validation rules to the same input or mode.
One proposal assumes a response shape, enum, or status code that the other would replace.
The backend proposal changes a contract while the frontend proposal invents a local substitute.
A preservation claim in one proposal conflicts with a modification in the other.
Both changes pass alone, but the scenarios require mutually exclusive UI or API states.

Consider the word “preserve.” The License Plate proposal might say that VIN behavior remains unchanged, while revise-vin-search exists specifically to change it. The two business goals need not conflict, but the preservation boundary has become stale. Revising that sentence could be as important as reconciling the request type because it changes what License Plate regression tests should prove.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.7 Choose a coordination response
Finding overlap does not automatically require one large change. Choose the response that keeps the business decision easiest to review:








Response
When it may fit
Artifact consequence




Keep both changes separate
The goals remain independently releasable after one shared decision
Revise each affected proposal, delta, design, and task list to record the decision


Establish a prerequisite
One change must define a contract or behavior before the other can be coherent
Record the dependency and review the dependent change against the new baseline


Combine the changes
Their scenarios cannot describe a complete outcome independently
Replace the two partial plans with one reviewed scope before more implementation


Pause one change
Product owners have not settled incompatible behavior
Keep the unresolved change active rather than encoding a decision through merge order



For this exercise, suppose reviewers choose a prerequisite rather than combining the changes. The VIN rule should become accepted first because the License Plate proposal promises to preserve VIN behavior and must test against the revised rule. License Plate remains a separate business capability, but its preservation boundary and generated-client tasks now depend on the VIN change.
That choice should appear in both active artifacts. The VIN design could identify the shared request contract it establishes. The License Plate proposal could replace its stale “VIN remains unchanged” assumption with the specific revised VIN behavior it must preserve. Its tasks could also defer final client generation until the reviewed backend contract contains both the accepted VIN rule and proposed plate fields.






NoteRecord the decision before moving code



A new reviewer should be able to recover the dependency from proposal.md, delta specifications, design.md, and tasks.md alone. If the answer depends on the originating chat transcript, the coordination decision has not reached the durable artifacts.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.8 Coordinate the backend-owned contract
In this book’s two-repository lab, the backend owns the OpenAPI contract and the Angular client is generated from it. That ownership suggests a coordination point even when implementation proceeds in parallel.
Frontend work could begin against reviewed scenarios and a proposed contract. Tests for the new mode control, empty states, or validation transitions need not wait for every backend task. Final client integration, however, should use a client generated from the contract the backend actually publishes. A hand-written TypeScript request type could make both branches compile while hiding the unresolved contract.
Before either change closes, reviewers could ask:

Can one request represent Unit Number, VIN, and License Plate without ambiguous combinations?
Which layer rejects a plate without jurisdiction or a VIN that violates the revised rule?
Does the OpenAPI document express the same modes and constraints as the backend behavior?
Has the Angular client been regenerated from that reviewed document?
Do frontend states distinguish invalid input, no match, and request failure as specified?

Answers shared by both changes may belong in the accepted search specification or a recorded contract decision. Answers unique to License Plate should remain in its delta. This division could keep one proposal from silently redefining every search mode.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
section: 15.9 Use worktrees without confusing their role
text:
15.9 Use worktrees without confusing their role
Separate worktrees may let a developer or agent keep both branches available at once:
git worktree add ../truck-search-license-plate -b feature/license-plate
git worktree add ../truck-search-vin -b feature/revise-vin
git worktree list
Each directory could have its own application code and OpenSpec change. Before creating them, check the repository’s branch names and destination paths; the example names may not fit an existing checkout.
Keep the accepted-baseline commit, change names, contract owner, dependency decision, and verification evidence in a place the team can recover outside those directories. Without that shared coordination record, two worktrees could merely let incompatible assumptions develop faster.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.10 Reconcile before synchronization or archive
Archive order may matter when the first archived change updates the main specifications that the second change originally assumed. Finishing first would be a weak ordering rule; a dependency or shared contract would offer a stronger reason.
Before accepting the VIN prerequisite, compare its delta with the main specification and inspect the proposed result. After synchronization or archive updates the accepted baseline, return to the License Plate change before applying or closing it:

Re-read its proposal and delta specifications against the updated main specs.
Replace preservation claims or scenarios that still describe the old VIN rule.
Revisit design decisions that depend on the shared request or response contract.
Reopen any completed task whose evidence came from the earlier baseline.
Run strict validation and the affected VIN regression tests again.
Apply, verify, and archive License Plate only after its artifacts describe the combined system.

If the team uses /opsx:sync to merge a reviewed delta into the main specifications while keeping the change active, the same comparison would still apply. Synchronization changes the baseline used by neighboring work; it does not prove that neighboring deltas remain coherent. Before accepting the sync, inspect the main-spec diff and keep the change active until its implementation and evidence are ready.
Silently rewriting License Plate code to accommodate the new VIN rule would leave its active artifacts stale. Another reviewer could not tell whether the behavior was intentional or merely the result of whichever branch merged last. Revising the proposal, scenarios, design, and tasks would turn that implementation adjustment back into a reviewable decision.

15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.11 Hands-on exercise
Create two active changes in the prepared truck-search repositories: one for License Plate search and one for a revision to VIN behavior.

Give each change a distinct business goal, scope, non-goals, and preservation boundary.
Record the accepted commit and main specifications used as their common baseline.
Validate both changes, then compare each delta with the baseline and with the other delta.
Complete the overlap worksheet for requirements, API contract, generated client, UI, validation, and regression tests.
Identify one semantic conflict that a clean Git merge would not settle.
Choose whether to keep, order, combine, or pause the changes, and record the reason in the affected artifacts.
Accept the prerequisite change, then revise the remaining change against the new baseline.
Apply and verify the remaining change without losing either reviewed business goal.

At each step, ask which artifact would let a reviewer recover the decision. A conflict discovered only after the first archive may indicate that the surviving change has become stale; it need not mean that parallel work itself was a mistake.

15  Coordinating Parallel Changes

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.12 Verification checkpoint
Check whether the final accepted specifications describe all search modes without contradictory input, validation, or result rules. Verify the artifacts and implementation from that question outward:
openspec validate --all
git diff -- openspec/specs openspec/changes
Then run the focused backend, contract-generation, frontend, and regression checks configured for the prepared repositories. The evidence should support these conclusions:

Each change retained a distinct, reviewed business purpose.
Shared requirements now have one interpretation.
The accepted specifications contain the reconciled VIN and License Plate behavior.
The generated Angular client came from the reviewed backend contract.
Unit Number, VIN, and License Plate scenarios pass at the affected boundaries.
No active artifact still assumes the pre-coordination baseline.

If the final item fails, keep that change active. Updating the stale artifact and repeating the focused checks would cost less than archiving a contradiction that the next change must untangle.

title: 15  Coordinating Parallel Changes
text:
15.13 What you learned
Separate change folders, branches, and worktrees can isolate activity. A common baseline and a sideways delta review can then expose incompatible intent. Once overlap appears, record the shared decision, order changes by dependency, and recheck the surviving proposal after the baseline moves.
Choose that coordination point before merge repair. Once Git reports the textual conflict, it may be too late to recover the unrecorded product decision from the changed lines alone.

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.1 Learning objective
A developer finishes an OpenSpec change, closes the Copilot session, and opens a pull request. The tests pass, the code looks reasonable, and every task has a checkmark. Yet the reviewer still has to ask what behavior changed, who approved it, and whether the Angular client came from the same contract as the Spring Boot implementation.
What separated this work from a private OpenSpec exercise? Not the number of artifact files. Ask whether another developer could enter after the original session disappeared and make the next correct decision. That person would need the business intent, accepted behavior, technical constraints, and verification evidence without depending on the author’s memory.
Treat that handoff as the test for team practice. Then agree on which changes deserve a spec, where decisions belong, who reviews them, and what evidence permits the work to move forward. Installing OpenSpec in every repository without that agreement may only create more places to disagree.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to introduce a proportionate OpenSpec workflow to a team, define its decision and review boundaries, and test whether the resulting record can support a developer who did not participate in the original Copilot session.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.2 Start with the handoff problem
The exercises used one person, two repositories, and a controlled sequence of changes. Now picture the commercial truck search moving through a delivery team. A product owner requests the search mode in Jira. One developer shapes the backend contract, another regenerates the Angular client, and a third reviews validation behavior. Interruptions and parallel work separate those steps.
Where should the next person look if “commercial truck” means something different in the ticket, delta specification, API schema, and UI test? Let Jira establish priority and ownership. Let the OpenSpec change record the proposed behavior and technical decisions. Let the repository preserve the reviewed result. Keep chat as working space rather than the only place where a decision exists.






NoteA practical test for shared context



Ask a reviewer to explain what should change, what should remain unchanged, and how the team will know the work is complete using repository artifacts alone. A “no” points to a handoff problem, even when the implementation passes its tests.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.3 Agree on the minimum operating model
text:
16.3 Agree on the minimum operating model
Before asking everyone to create artifacts, settle a few working rules. Which work requires an OpenSpec change? Who may accept behavior? When may implementation begin? What would count as enough verification to synchronize or archive?
Keep the first agreement short enough to scan during a change. A longer process document may be harder to apply and easier to ignore. Adapt the following example to the repository’s paths and commands:
## OpenSpec working agreement

- Create a full change for new behavior, contract changes, cross-repository work, and changes to
    accepted requirements.
- Link the change name from the Jira issue and pull request.
- Obtain behavior review before implementation when the proposal changes a user-visible outcome.
- Obtain technical review before implementation when the delta changes an API, persistence model,
    security boundary, or generated client.
- Keep decisions in OpenSpec artifacts; use chat and meetings to develop them.
- Record focused test commands and results before synchronization or archive.
- Recheck every active change after its accepted baseline moves.
Would every team choose those exact rules? Probably not. Match the approval and evidence burden to the product’s constraints. Keep the boundary explicit so people and agents can see where a lightweight record ends and a reviewed change begins.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.4 Give each system one job
Teams often lose intent because the same decision appears in several tools with slightly different wording. Copying the full requirement into Jira, a proposal, a pull request, and a chat prompt may look thorough, but which copy would be corrected after review?
A clearer division might look like this:








System or artifact
Question it should answer
What it should avoid becoming




Jira issue
Why is the work scheduled, who owns it, and what is its status?
The only source of detailed behavior


proposal.md
What outcome is proposed, what is in scope, and what is excluded?
A duplicate task board


Delta specifications
Which observable behavior would be added, modified, or removed?
An implementation diary


design.md
Which technical choices and constraints shape the implementation?
A restatement of every requirement


tasks.md
In what order could the team implement and verify the change?
Evidence that unchecked behavior is acceptable


Pull request
What code and artifact revisions are ready for review?
The first place a product decision appears


Tests and verification record
What evidence supports the reviewed behavior?
A substitute for deciding what the behavior should be



Do not eliminate links between tools; make them directional. Point from the Jira issue to the OpenSpec change for behavior. Point from the pull request to both, then record the verification commands there or in the change. Reviewers can follow that chain without comparing several competing copies of the requirement.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.5 Walk one change through the team
text:
16.5 Walk one change through the team
Test the shared workflow against one change. Suppose the product owner requests commercial truck search across the Spring Boot and Angular repositories. How might that request move without turning OpenSpec into a sequence of gates for their own sake?

16.5.1 Frame the proposal together
Begin with the business goal, affected behavior, non-goals, and known repository boundaries. Use an exploration session to uncover current routes, generated client code, and existing search scenarios. Do not ask the agent to decide what counts as a commercial truck; assign that definition to an accountable human owner.
Focus the early review on meaning rather than prose quality:

Would two reviewers interpret “commercial truck” the same way?
Which current search modes must remain unchanged?
Does the request alter a public contract or only add a client-side filter?
Which repository owns the contract from which the client is generated?
What outcome should occur for invalid input, no match, and service failure?

Resolve those questions while changing the proposal remains cheap. Waiting until pull-request review may turn the same disagreement into code rework across both repositories.


16.5.2 Review behavior before design hardens
Once the proposal and delta scenarios express the requested outcome, ask the product or domain reviewer to accept the behavior boundary. Leave class names, endpoint paths, and component structure to technical review unless those choices affect the product contract.
Next, examine design.md and the cross-repository implications with the technical reviewer. Would the backend publish the OpenAPI change before the frontend regenerates its client? Could old and new clients coexist during deployment? Which validation belongs in the API, and which feedback belongs in the UI? Let those answers shape the implementation plan without reopening an already settled business outcome.


16.5.3 Turn tasks into handoff points
A private checklist may follow whatever order helps its author. For a team task list, show where work passes to someone else and what must be true at that point.
For the commercial truck change, a useful sequence could include:

Review the behavior and non-goals with the named business owner.
Review the proposed request and response contract with backend and frontend owners.
Implement and test the backend behavior against the reviewed scenarios.
Publish the contract artifact and regenerate the Angular client from it.
Implement the UI states and run focused frontend tests.
Compare the implementation, generated artifacts, and accepted scenarios before archive.

Give each step a verification point rather than a bare completion claim. “Regenerate the client” says what to do. “Regenerate from the reviewed backend contract and confirm no hand-written request type remains” gives the next reviewer something to inspect.


16.5.4 Preserve the review result
Approval in a meeting or chat may unblock the author, but would it help the developer who takes over next week? Record the result in the artifact that governs the behavior or design. Skip the meeting transcript; preserve enough context to prevent the same question from returning during implementation.
Carry the OpenSpec change name into commits and pull requests. Name the commands run and any checks that remain outside automation. After synchronization or archive, ask whether the accepted specifications describe the behavior without requiring the active change folder.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.6 Match review ownership to the decision
text:
16.6 Match review ownership to the decision
Would every artifact need a separate approver? That rule could add delay without improving the decision. Review ownership may work better when it follows the consequence under review.








Decision
Likely reviewer
Review question




User-visible behavior and non-goals
Product or domain owner
Is this the outcome the system should promise?


API, data, security, or deployment boundary
Technical owner
Can the design preserve the required constraints?


Code and automated tests
Implementation reviewer
Does the implementation satisfy the reviewed scenarios?


Synchronization and archive readiness
Change owner or release reviewer
Do accepted specs, implementation, and evidence now agree?



One person may cover several rows on a small team. Still, name the decision behind each approval. A product owner accepting endpoint naming does not replace technical review, and code approval does not settle an ambiguous business rule.
Define escalation points for consequences that need a specific owner, such as a new public API, a removed scenario, a security boundary, or disagreement between active changes. Keep routine edits with the normal reviewer. Let consequence, rather than title or artifact count, determine the review path.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.7 Scale the workflow to the risk
text:
16.7 Scale the workflow to the risk
Requiring the same artifact set for a typo and a cross-repository contract change would teach the team to work around the process. How much specification would help before its maintenance cost exceeds the uncertainty it removes?
Use a simple classification to discuss that choice:








Change shape
Possible record
Typical review




Existing behavior, low risk, easy to reverse
Issue or pull-request note tied to accepted specs
Implementation review


Local behavior with bounded impact
Proposal, delta scenarios, and focused tasks
Behavior and implementation review


Contract, security, persistence, or cross-repository change
Full proposal, deltas, design, tasks, and verification record
Named behavior and technical review


Urgent production repair
Small initial record with owner, risk, and verification, followed by artifact repair
Immediate peer review and scheduled follow-up



Do not let the matrix make the decision automatically. Use it to expose uncertainty, reversibility, blast radius, contract impact, and the cost of discovering a mistake late. When a smaller artifact set seems sufficient, record the exception so the reviewer can challenge the reason rather than wonder whether files were forgotten.






WarningCeremony can hide missing thought



A complete folder may still contain vague requirements, copied design text, and tasks that prove only that files changed. Review the decisions and scenarios, not the presence of filenames. A smaller record with a precise boundary could serve the team better than a full set of unexamined artifacts.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
section: 16.8 Make Copilot work from reviewed context
text:
16.8 Make Copilot work from reviewed context
Once a team shares artifacts, start Copilot prompts from reviewed material rather than each developer’s reconstruction of the ticket. This only works while the repository context remains current.
Ask Copilot to compare implementation with accepted scenarios, identify a contract boundary, or draft tests for review. Point to the relevant proposal, delta, design, and repository instructions. State where the agent must stop and request a human decision.
Read the active `add-commercial-truck-search` artifacts and the accepted truck-search specs.

Report any mismatch between the proposed scenarios, backend contract, generated Angular client,
and current tests.  Do not choose new product behavior or edit accepted specifications.  List any
decision that requires the product owner or API owner.
Would another developer find the same governing requirements and unresolved decisions from the same repository state? If the answer depends on instructions held in one person’s prompt history, move those instructions into maintained repository context.
Review that context after changes to OpenSpec, Copilot customization files, generated-client commands, or test tooling. Run the documented commands, remove contradictory instructions, and revise examples whose paths or behavior changed.
crumbs: Part IV: Change Under Pressure
16  Making SDD a Team Practice

title: 16  Making SDD a Team Practice
text:
16.9 Introduce the practice in stages
A team may resist SDD for reasonable reasons. The artifacts take time, reviewers can become a bottleneck, and poorly scoped specs can freeze choices that implementation still needs to explore. Starting with every repository and every change could make those costs arrive before the team sees the handoff benefit.
Gather evidence with a limited pilot:

Choose one capability with a real handoff or cross-repository boundary.
Agree on the minimum rules and name the reviewers before opening the change.
Run two or three changes through proposal, implementation, verification, and archive.
Ask a developer outside the work to reconstruct one completed change from repository artifacts.
Revise the agreement where the handoff failed or where an artifact added no useful decision.

Measure friction in concrete terms. Which questions returned during code review? Which decisions had no owner? Which artifact became stale first? Where did a reviewer still need the author or chat transcript? Those observations say more than a count of created spec files.
Teams might also watch for signs that the practice is becoming performative:

Proposals appear after the code and merely describe it.
Reviewers approve artifact folders without reading scenarios.
Jira and OpenSpec contain competing versions of the same behavior.
tasks.md records activity but no verification.
Active changes remain based on specifications that have since moved.
Archive becomes a cleanup chore disconnected from acceptance.

Any one occurrence may have a reasonable explanation. When a pattern repeats, revise the working agreement, training, or scope.

16.10 Capstone: establish a team workflow
Use a proposed commercial truck search change to test the operating model across the Spring Boot and Angular repositories. The goal is not the largest possible artifact set. Could the team defend the amount of specification, transfer the work between people, and recover the final decision later?

Name the business owner, technical owner, change author, and implementation reviewer.
Record the business goal, affected behavior, non-goals, and accepted baseline.
Classify the change by uncertainty, reversibility, blast radius, and contract impact.
Choose the OpenSpec artifacts required by that classification and record any exception.
Review the delta scenarios before implementation begins.
Record the backend-owned contract boundary and the generated-client handoff.
Divide tasks.md at points where responsibility or evidence passes between team members.
Link the Jira issue, OpenSpec change, commits, pull requests, and verification results.
Complete the verification checkpoint before synchronization or archive.

16.11 Verification checkpoint
Give the completed change to a reviewer who did not participate in its Copilot sessions. Without asking the original author, could that reviewer answer the following questions?

What user-visible behavior changed, and what remained outside scope?
Who accepted the behavior and the technical boundary?
Which accepted requirements and delta scenarios governed the implementation?
Which repository owned the contract, and how was the Angular client produced?
What verification evidence supports synchronization and archive?
Which unresolved risks or follow-up items remain?

Run the structural checks available in the repository as supporting evidence:
openspec status --change add-commercial-truck-search
openspec validate add-commercial-truck-search --strict
openspec show add-commercial-truck-search --diff
Then run the focused backend, contract-generation, frontend, and regression checks named in the change. Structural validation could show that OpenSpec can parse the artifacts; it could not show that the right people made the missing product decision.
If the reviewer cannot reconstruct the work, repair the smallest broken handoff. The missing piece may be an owner, a scenario, a contract dependency, a verification result, or a link. If the reviewer can reconstruct it but the process felt heavier than the risk justified, revise the working agreement before applying it to the next class of change.

title: 17  Summary
text:
OpenSpec gives an AI-assisted team a durable place to keep intent, but the files alone do not create alignment. The team must still ask precise questions, review generated artifacts, test the implementation, and reconcile overlapping decisions.
The truck-search sequence demonstrates the core patterns:

A greenfield change establishes the first accepted behavior through explore, propose, apply, and archive.
An additive delta introduces VIN search without replacing unit-number search.
A modified delta replaces the old unit-number constraint with a maximum of 10 characters.
An active proposal can be revised before implementation when the business changes direction.
Parallel changes require both artifact isolation and source-control isolation, followed by deliberate synchronization.

The practical test is whether a developer or agent can enter the repository in a later session and recover what the system should do, what is changing, and how completion will be verified. When the specs, code, and tests answer those questions consistently, context has become shared engineering material rather than chat history.

A.2 Lab Setup

A.2.1 Required tools
Plan to have these available for each participant:

Windows 11 or macOS;

Before the class, check the current OpenSpec installation instructions at https://openspec.dev/docs/installation. Tool versions and package commands can change.


A.2.2 Prepare the exercise repositories
Start by cloning the prepared backend and frontend repositories. It may help to confirm that each repository builds and passes its tests before initializing OpenSpec. The backend owns the OpenAPI contract, and OpenAPI Generator produces the TypeScript Angular client used by the frontend.
cd commercial-truck-search-api
openspec init

cd ../commercial-truck-search-ui
openspec init
When initialization asks which AI tool to configure, select GitHub Copilot. Give each repository its own context instead of copying one configuration into both repositories.
The backend configuration records Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1, Maven, Spring Data JPA, H2, test conventions, and ownership of the OpenAPI contract. The frontend configuration records Angular 21, generated-client boundaries, Vitest, Angular component tests, and Playwright.
Review the generated configuration. It can describe stable project facts, but it should not invent database products, deployment platforms, or business rules that the class has not selected.


A.2.3 Preflight check
Before Morning 1, check that:

Both starter applications build and their existing tests pass.
openspec init created the expected project files in both repositories.
GitHub Copilot Chat recognizes the expected OpenSpec commands in VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA.
Each participant knows which commands belong in the terminal and which belong in chat.
Each repository has a clean baseline commit suitable for reset between exercises.

You may want to keep prepared checkpoints for both repositories after each major exercise. That gives participants who miss a step a way to resume from the same accepted specs, contracts, and code state as the rest of the class.

A.3 Troubleshooting OpenSpec

A.3.1 A diagnostic method
For each problem, start with the symptom and a likely cause. Then run the cheapest check that could distinguish between possible causes before choosing a repair. Keep the command output from that check; it may be more useful than repeating a setup step that could change the evidence.


A.3.2 Installation failures
You might see one of these symptoms:

openspec cannot be found after npm installation.
The terminal resolves a different global npm location than expected.
Windows execution policy or macOS permissions prevent the command from running.
The installed version differs from the book’s 1.13.1 baseline.



A.3.3 Initialization and update failures
Check whether:

OpenSpec initialized a different directory than expected.
Existing generated files conflict with the update.
The selected GitHub Copilot integration or profile is unavailable.
Project-owned configuration changed unexpectedly.



A.3.4 Command discovery failures
You may be dealing with command discovery when:

VS Code does not show the expected prompt command.
IntelliJ IDEA does not discover the same workflow.
A prompt-file command is being confused with an Agent Skill or terminal CLI command.
The IDE appears to be using an earlier version of the generated integration files.



A.3.5 Artifact and validation failures
The failure may be in artifact or validation handling when:

A change cannot identify its schema.
Artifact dependencies remain blocked.
Requirements or scenarios fail strict validation.
A modified requirement does not match the accepted source requirement.
Archive or sync encounters overlapping deltas.



A.3.6 Two-repository failures
Compare the repositories when:

Frontend and backend changes use different business terms.
The generated Angular client appears stale.
The OpenAPI document does not match the backend behavior.
A test passes against a different backend or port than the one you intended.



A.3.7 Recovery boundaries
Before regeneration, preserve project-owned specs and active changes. Use version control to inspect generated-file changes. If an OpenSpec defect remains reproducible, report the version, operating system, minimal repository state, command, and complete output.

B.1 OpenSpec CLI Command Reference
This section offers a quick reference for the openspec CLI commands used throughout the book. For OpenSpec slash commands, see the next section. The CLI command names and examples are current as of OpenSpec CLI 1.13.1. Since your installed version may differ, you may want to run openspec --help or openspec <command> --help to check the syntax available to you.
The CLI helps manage the files and relationships that make a change reviewable. Decisions about a change’s scope and the quality of its requirements remain with the people reviewing the work.

title: Appendix B — OpenSpec Reference
text:
B.1.1 Typical workflow

You might run openspec init once in a project, then use openspec update when the generated instruction files need to catch up.
To begin a change, use openspec new change <name>, then inspect its artifact status with openspec status --change <name>.
You can use openspec list, openspec show, openspec context, and openspec instructions to inspect the repository and work out what an agent needs next.
Before treating the change as ready, consider running openspec validate <name>. In CI, openspec validate --all may be a better fit when the repository is the unit of validation.
After implementation and verification, you can run openspec archive <name>. Archiving updates the main specifications and moves the completed change out of the active work area.

OpenSpec reports failures through the process exit status, which makes commands such as validate suitable for scripts and CI. The CLI help does not promise a numbered list of exit codes, so this reference does not invent one. In a pipeline, treat a nonzero status as a failed check and preserve the command output as the diagnostic.


B.1.2 Core commands
The commands below cover the operations most projects use regularly. The --json options can help when another tool needs to consume a result, but reading the Markdown artifacts still matters during review.








Command
Purpose
Useful options




openspec init [path]
Initialize OpenSpec in a project and write the selected tool instruction files.
--tools all, --tools github-copilot, --language <language>, --profile <profile>, --force


openspec update [path]
Update OpenSpec instruction files after the CLI or tool configuration changes.
--force


openspec new change <name>
Create a new change directory using the selected workflow schema.
--description <text>, --goal <text>, --schema <name>, --store <id>, --json


openspec list
List active changes.
--changes, --specs, --sort recent|name, --json, --store <id>


openspec show [item-name]
Display a change or specification.
--type change|spec, --json, --diff, --deltas-only, --store <id>


openspec status --change <id>
Show which artifacts are complete for a change.
--all, --schema <name>, --json, --store <id>


openspec validate [item-name]
Validate a change or specification.
--all, --changes, --specs, --strict, --json, --type change|spec, --store <id>


openspec archive [change-name]
Archive a completed change and update the main specifications.
--yes, --skip-specs, --no-validate, --json, --store <id>


openspec doctor
Report relationship health for the resolved OpenSpec root.
--json, --store <id>



The command names reflect two related interfaces. openspec new change creates a change. The older grouped forms, openspec change show, openspec change list, and openspec change validate, can inspect and validate changes. Since the help output marks openspec change list as deprecated, new scripts are better served by the top-level list, show, and validate commands.
For a quick inspection of a repository, you could start with:
openspec list
openspec status --all
openspec doctor
For a CI (continuous integration) check that covers both active and archived material, choose the narrowest validation that matches the pipeline’s purpose. openspec validate --all validates all changes and specifications, while openspec validate --archived checks that archived changes have completed tasks.


B.1.3 Store and workset commands
Stores and worksets address different needs. You can think of a store as a standalone OpenSpec repository registered on the local machine, giving several related projects a shared place for specifications and changes. A workset is a personal, local view that composes folders for a working session. Removing a workset does not remove its member folders.








Command
Purpose
Useful options




openspec store setup [id]
Create and register a local store.
--path <path>, --remote <url>, --init-git, --no-init-git, --json


openspec store register [path]
Register an existing local store.
--id <id>, --yes, --json


openspec store list
List stores registered on this machine.
--json


openspec store doctor [id]
Check a store’s registration and metadata.
--json


openspec store unregister <id>
Forget a registration without deleting the files.
--json


openspec store remove <id>
Forget a registration and delete its local folder.
--yes, --json


openspec context
Print the working context for the resolved OpenSpec root.
--json, --store <id>, --code-workspace <path>, --force


openspec workset create [name]
Save a named view of project folders.
Repeat --member <path>; optionally use --tool <id> and --json


openspec workset list
Show saved worksets and their members.
--json


openspec workset open <name>
Open a saved workset in its preferred tool.
--json


openspec workset remove <name>
Delete a saved workset without touching member folders.
--json



When the working root should come from a registered store rather than the current project, you can add --store <id> to commands that support it. If shared context is missing or unexpectedly empty, it may help to run openspec store doctor first. That checks the registration boundary before you inspect individual artifacts.






WarningOpenSpec Stores are still in BETA



Please keep in mind the OpenSpec Stores feature is still in BETA release and may change before they are released as a production feature in OpenSpec.

text:
B.3 OpenSpec schema.yaml and Template Reference
OpenSpec uses Schemas to configure how an OpenSpec workflow executes. This section can help when you need to read or change an OpenSpec workflow. It covers the fields in schema.yaml, the dependency rules between artifacts, and the way templates become generated change files.

B.3.1 Schema fields
An OpenSpec schema defines a planning workflow in YAML. It names the workflow, lists the artifacts it produces, and describes the handoff from planning to implementation. In the built-in spec-driven schema, the default sequence is explicit: proposal leads to specs and design, and tasks depends on both before implementation can begin.
The top-level fields are:









Field
Type
Required?
Effect




name
string
Yes
Names the schema. OpenSpec uses the schema directory as the lookup key, even if this value differs.


version
positive integer
Yes
Records the schema revision. It does not change OpenSpec behavior by itself.


description
string
No
Describes the workflow when schemas are listed.


artifacts
non-empty list
Yes
Declares the planning artifacts and their dependencies.


apply
mapping
No
Defines what must be complete before implementation starts and, optionally, which task file tracks progress.



Each entry in artifacts defines one document or one set of documents:









Field
Type
Required?
Effect




id
unique string
Yes
Identifies the artifact. Other artifacts and apply use this value in requires.


generates
relative path or glob
Yes
Tells OpenSpec where the artifact is written inside the change folder. For example, specs/**/*.md can produce one spec per capability.


description
string
Yes
Labels the artifact in the guidance given to the agent.


template
relative path
Yes
Selects the Markdown template under the schema’s templates/ directory.


instruction
string
No
Gives the agent artifact-specific guidance, such as whether the document explains why, what, or how.


requires
list of artifact IDs
No
Makes this artifact wait until the named artifacts are complete. The default is an empty list.



It is useful to treat requires as a dependency graph rather than a suggested reading order. OpenSpec marks an artifact ready only after every dependency is complete. It rejects missing IDs, duplicate IDs, and dependency cycles. When several artifacts are ready at once, their order in artifacts determines which one OpenSpec returns first.
The generates value is relative to the active change directory. proposal.md therefore produces openspec/changes/<change-name>/proposal.md, while specs/**/*.md matches Markdown files below that change’s specs/ directory. Completion is structural: OpenSpec checks that the expected file exists, or that a glob matches at least one file. The check does not evaluate the document’s content.
The optional apply block controls the planning-to-implementation handoff. Its requires field names the artifacts that must exist before apply is ready. Its tracks field points to a relative Markdown file in the change directory, normally tasks.md. OpenSpec uses task checkboxes in that file to report whether work is blocked, ready, or complete. An optional instruction replaces the built-in guidance sent to the implementation agent.
The default workflow has this essential shape:
name: spec-driven
version: 1
description: Default OpenSpec workflow - proposal -> specs -> design -> tasks
artifacts:
  - id: proposal
    generates: proposal.md
    description: Initial proposal document outlining the change
    template: proposal.md
    requires: []
  - id: specs
    generates: specs/**/*.md
    description: Detailed specifications for the change
    template: spec.md
    requires:
      - proposal
  - id: design
    generates: design.md
    description: Technical design document with implementation details
    template: design.md
    requires:
      - proposal
  - id: tasks
    generates: tasks.md
    description: Implementation checklist with trackable tasks
    template: tasks.md
    requires:
      - specs
      - design
apply:
  requires:
    - tasks
  tracks: tasks.md
The example omits the longer agent instructions. The fields serve different purposes: description labels the artifact, template supplies its output shape, and instruction explains what the agent should produce. A changed dependency changes the workflow; a changed template changes the starting structure of every new artifact created from it.


B.3.2 Template structure
A schema directory contains schema.yaml and a templates/ directory. OpenSpec resolves the template value in each artifact entry relative to that directory:
openspec/schemas/spec-driven/
├── schema.yaml
└── templates/
    ├── proposal.md
    ├── spec.md
    ├── design.md
    └── tasks.md
Templates are Markdown skeletons rather than files copied into the change directory. OpenSpec gives the selected template to the agent as its expected output format. The agent fills that structure and writes the result at the path named by generates.
In the default schema, the mapping is:









Artifact
Template
Generated path
Purpose




proposal
proposal.md
proposal.md
Explains why the change is needed, what it changes, its capabilities, and its impact.


specs
spec.md
specs/<capability-path>/spec.md
Defines observable behavior through requirements and scenarios.


design
design.md
design.md
Explains how the change will be implemented, including decisions, risks, and trade-offs.


tasks
tasks.md
tasks.md
Breaks the implementation into ordered, checkable work items.



The specs entry is the exception to the one-file pattern. It allows a change to produce one delta specification for each capability named by the proposal. The proposal establishes the reason and scope, the spec files define behavior, the design records the technical approach, and the task list turns the plan into work the apply phase can track. Keeping these roles separate helps prevent implementation details from replacing requirements.
When a team needs different documents or a different sequence, it can create a project schema under openspec/schemas/<name>/, edit schema.yaml and the matching templates, and run openspec schema validate <name> before using it. Forking the built-in spec-driven schema copies its schema definition, templates, and instructions into a project-owned directory. A custom template changes the structure of future artifacts; a schema dependency changes which artifacts can be drafted and when. Built-in schemas ship with OpenSpec, so forking one before editing it is preferable to modifying the package copy.

text:
B.4 Further Reading and Community Resources
OpenSpec is open-source software available through its GitHub project and repository. Those resources include an issue queue and discussions, which can provide information about OpenSpec and Spec-Driven Development more generally.

B.4.1 Official documentation
The OpenSpec repository and its documentation are useful starting points. The OPSX workflow describes the workflow used throughout this book. The installation guide covers setup, while supported tools and aliases lists the available integrations.
These sources cover the mechanics of using OpenSpec. Your repository’s proposal, requirements, design, tasks, and verification evidence still provide the context for a specific change. The documentation can explain how a command works, but it cannot decide whether the change is understood well enough to implement or whether the resulting behavior is correct. Your project team remains responsible for the specs, and OpenSpec is more useful when the team understands them fully.


B.4.2 Community schemas and extensions
Community-built schemas and extensions may help when the official OpenSpec workflow does not cover a particular business domain or team practice. They can also provide a working example. It is useful to treat each community-built schema as a proposal to evaluate: read its source and examples, check its maintenance activity and compatibility with your OpenSpec version, and identify the assumptions it makes about your repository and development process.
A small, representative change can provide a useful trial before the schema becomes a team convention. It helps to ask whether its artifacts make requirements easier to review, give Copilot useful context, and produce evidence that the implementation matches the intended behavior. If it adds more SDD ceremony without improving those checks, you might cherry-pick the useful ideas from the community-built schema and leave the rest behind. Recording adopted conventions in the repository gives the next developer a way to understand them.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Resources
text:
C.1.1 Explore unit-number search

/opsx:explore We are considering an initial commercial truck search capability. Could users search by a 15-character unit number? Please ask about exact versus partial matching, case handling, invalid input, no-match behavior, and the response shown in the UI. Hold off on creating change artifacts until those decisions are clear.



C.1.2 Propose unit-number search

/opsx:propose add-unit-number-search Based on the exploration decisions, could you draft the proposal? Please keep implementation choices out of the behavioral requirements and include scenarios for valid input, invalid input, a match, and no match.



C.1.3 Add VIN search

/opsx:propose add-vin-search-option Could we add a secondary search mode for a 17-character VIN while preserving unit-number search? Please ask how users would select the mode and how the two modes should share response behavior. Represent the new capability as an additive delta.



C.1.4 Modify unit-number validation

/opsx:propose update-unit-number-length We are considering replacing the current unit-number length rule with a maximum of 10 characters. Could you identify every scenario that would change and every existing behavior that should remain intact? Represent the replacement as a modified requirement.



C.1.5 Update an active filter proposal

/opsx:update Could you revise the active origin-state filter change to include Active Status with values Active and Decommissioned? Please update the proposal, requirements and scenarios, design, and tasks, and flag any unanswered question about how the filters should combine.



C.1.6 Review generated artifacts

Could you review this OpenSpec change without editing it? Please report contradictions, unsupported assumptions, missing edge cases, tasks that do not trace to requirements, and requirements that lack verification tasks.



C.1.7 Verify before archive

Could you compare the implemented change with the active delta and task list before archiving? Please identify unmet scenarios, code outside the approved scope, stale tasks, and tests that do not prove the specified behavior. Hold off on archiving the change.

C.2 Artifact Review Checklists

C.2.1 Proposal

Does it make the business problem and intended outcome clear?
Is the scope narrow enough to review and implement with confidence?
Does it call out the exclusions that matter for this change?
Does it leave out technical assumptions that have not been approved?
Could a reviewer tell whether this adds behavior or modifies what is already accepted?



C.2.2 Requirements and scenarios

Does each requirement describe behavior that someone could observe?
Are terms such as “maximum,” “exact,” and “optional” clear enough to avoid ambiguity?
Do the scenarios cover successful, invalid, and empty outcomes where those cases matter?
Would an additive delta leave existing behavior unchanged?
Does a modified delta include the full replacement requirement?
Could each scenario become an automated or repeatable test?



C.2.3 Design

Does it focus on decisions that have implementation consequences?
Does it explain the API, UI, validation, and persistence boundaries that may be affected?
Does it identify compatibility or migration concerns that reviewers may need to consider?
Does it record tradeoffs instead of presenting one choice as inevitable?
Does it keep from duplicating behavioral requirements?



C.2.4 Tasks

Would each task produce a visible code, test, or documentation result?
Could each requirement be traced to implementation and verification work?
Are the tasks ordered in a way that reflects their dependencies?
Are the review and test steps clear enough to follow?
Would a new agent session be able to tell what remains incomplete?



C.2.5 Apply review

Does the implementation appear to match the latest artifacts rather than an earlier chat message?
Are the frontend and backend validation rules consistent with one another?
Do the tests demonstrate the scenarios rather than only executing lines?
Has the agent changed code outside the approved scope?
Does the task list reflect what has actually been completed?



C.2.6 Archive readiness

Has the team accepted the final behavior?
Do the affected tests pass?
Would the main spec remain coherent after the delta merges?
Have overlapping active changes been reviewed against the new baseline?
Is any unfinished work represented by a separate tracked change?

C.3 Instructor Guide

C.3.1 Course shape
Each morning is planned for 90 minutes and follows the same rhythm: establish one concept, demonstrate one artifact transition, let participants perform it, and review the resulting evidence.

C.3.2 Teaching checkpoints
It may help to measure progress by more than whether the agent generated files. Pause at these points:

After exploration, ask which ambiguities a person resolved.
After proposal, invite participants to separate behavior from implementation.
After apply, consider tracing one scenario through UI, API, persistence, and test code.
After archive, read the main spec without referring to the completed delta.



C.3.3 Expected friction
Participants may type slash commands into the terminal, accept generated assumptions, or treat task checkmarks as test results. Keeping the terminal/chat distinction visible can help, as can asking for an artifact review before each apply or archive step.
Tool output may differ across OpenSpec releases or coding-agent models. Teach the invariant workflow and review criteria rather than requiring identical generated prose.


C.3.4 Recovery points
Maintain three instructor baselines:

Baseline A: Initialized project with no truck-search spec.
Baseline B: Archived unit-number search.
Baseline C: Archived VIN search and 10-character unit-number rule.

These baselines can keep a setup problem from consuming the next morning. They also let the instructor demonstrate a delta against a known source of truth.


C.3.5 Closing discussion
Ask participants to name one change in their own codebase where conflicting interpretations would cost more than writing a short spec. Then ask for one change too small or reversible to justify the workflow. The contrast can help keep SDD grounded as an engineering tradeoff rather than a universal ceremony.
